📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A flaw fixed in Node.js this week lets unauthenticated clients crash servers that use the runtime's built-in HTTP/2 support on the 24.x and 26.x release lines. A second HTTP/2 flaw can cause a server to send a client pieces of its memory, including responses intended for other connections.

Fixed versions were released for all three supported lines: 22.23.5, 24.22.3, and 26.13.1.

The crash flaw, CVE-2026-123863, needs only a default HTTP/2 server that replies before the request body has fully arrived. The Node.js project calls that behavior typical. The crash works over both TLS and cleartext connections.

Recent findings suggest that the memory flaw, CVE-2026-123866, affects all three lines. From 24.22.0 and 26.9.0 onward, a client alone can trigger it. On 22.x and older 24.x and 26.x builds, it can still be triggered when the server itself closes a stream partway through a response, for example after an idle timeout.

Industry observers note that A separate flaw in Node.js HTTPS servers, CVE-2026-123864, can allow an unauthenticated client to read memory from other connections, "including TLS private keys and other people' requests," the project indicates. It affects all three supported lines.

In a recent development, the flaw needs a handler that calls res.flushHeaders() before the request body has fully arrived and later calls res.end() with data. Reading the leaked memory also needs a route that sends back or stores a request body. Plain HTTP servers built with node:http are not affected.

The release fixes 16 vulnerabilities in Node.js itself, seven of them rated high. The other four high-rated flaws, and the servers they affect, are:.

The eight flaws above are all in Node.js's own HTTP/2, HTTPS and TLS server code, so they matter where a Node.js process accepts those connections itself.

Updating to the fixed version for each line is the only fix in the project's security advisory. It lists no workaround for servers that cannot update yet.

End-of-life lines, including 20.x and 25.x, get no fix in this release, and the project says such versions are always affected.

According to recent reports, the advisory does not report any attacks using the flaws. It also does not say whether servers that met the conditions for the HTTPS flaw should replace their TLS keys or other secrets after updating.

Five of the flaws, including CVE-2026-123863 and CVE-2026-123864, were reported by Chris Rohlf in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research, according to the advisory.

Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability.
  • Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.
  • DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Open Source DocumentDB 1.0 Reaches General Availability.

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.

DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol. Most MongoDB drivers, tools, and queries work without changes.

DocumentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension that provides MongoDB API-compatible functionality and a gateway that translates MongoDB protocol requests into PostgreSQL calls. Version 1.0 supports PostgreSQL 15–18 through container images, with Linux packages available for PostgreSQL 17 and 18, and includes a Kubernetes operator, with the GA focusing on security, stability, and fixes for indexing, aggregation, and geospatial queries.

Microsoft confirmed the open source project early in 2025, aiming to provide the developer community with a NoSQL datastore built on PostgreSQL, and offering full visibility into the engine's architecture and implementation. The project joined the Linux Foundation a few months later, with support from other large database organizations including AWS, Cockroach Labs, Google, Snowflake, and Yugabyte. In the recent article "DocumentDB and the MIT License: What to Know Before You Build, Deploy, and Distribute," the team explains how DocumentDB’s permissive MIT license allows commercial use, modification, and hosting without requiring disclosure of proprietary code, contrasting it with MongoDB’s SSPL.

In a recent development, even if the project provides a page discussing the DocumentDB name disambiguation, covering the open source project, Azure DocumentDB, and Azure Cosmos DB, the community remains perplexed about the choice. In a popular Hacker News thread, user marifjeren writes:.

Name it anything else for god's sake. DocumentDB is already what everybody calls Amazon DocumentDB.

Sources indicate that with multiple open source options now on the market, Patty Chow, product manager at Microsoft, explains why open-source document databases need multiple implementations to give developers more choice in deployment and infrastructure while preserving compatibility with MongoDB drivers and queries. Chow writes:.

Sources indicate that mongoDB has given developers a widely used way to work with document data. Familiar drivers and query patterns are worth preserving. Alternative implementations give developers a chance to keep using that knowledge while evaluating different approaches to storage and deployment.

Industry observers note that in a Reddit thread, some practitioners raise concerns about current MongoDB compatibility and confusion with similarly named products. User 716green comments:.

It has been revealed that compatibility between MongoDB and FerretDB has been absolutely minimal compared to what you would probably expect. I've been a fan of DocumentDB for a long time and I love that Microsoft is supporting FerretDB.

DocumentDB provides the PostgreSQL extensions and its own MongoDB-compatible gateway, while FerretDB is a separate project that uses the DocumentDB extensions as its backend and provides its own MongoDB-compatible interface.

Layerbase recently ran an initial comparison of FerretDB and the PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB using YCSB benchmarks, finding that DocumentDB delivered 20–33% higher read throughput, while FerretDB had lower tail latency for updates in mixed workloads, but noting the results are not conclusive. An open GitHub matter reports higher query latency in DocumentDB 1.0 than MongoDB 9.0.4 across several workloads, but the results have not been independently verified.

Industry observers note that the DocumentDB release notes include upgrade paths and known issues. The project intends separate long-term support and development tracks, with its versioning policy still under discussion.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

#170. How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3045 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jad is an independent JavaScript & Web Performance consultant and educator who has trained developers worldwide through online platforms, in-person … More about Jad ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Most of us install a dependency once and never look at it again. It does its job, the tests pass, and we move on. But the web platform keeps moving too, and a surprising number of the libraries sitting in your package.json today are now built into the browser.

In a typical mid-sized JavaScript app, you can often find somewhere between 60KB and 90KB (minified and gzipped) of dependencies that the platform can now handle on its own. Date and number formatting, HTTP requests, modals, tooltips, deep cloning, grouping arrays: these were all real gaps a few years ago. A lot of them aren’t gaps anymore.

The reason those libraries stick around isn’t laziness. It’s that most teams don’t re-audit their dependencies on a Baseline cadence, or are simply not aware of how fast browsers are shipping these days. You check npm audit for security, but is this library still doing something the browser can’t? is a question that rarely gets asked. So the libraries stay.

In this article, we’ll run that audit together. Instead of going through dependencies one by one, we’ll work in clusters, because the wins tend to come in groups. We’ll do the bundle math, build a small decision framework you can reuse, and stay honest about the cases where the platform still falls short. By the end, you’ll have a repeatable process you can run on your own package.json.

Before we start deleting things, let’s quickly recap what Baseline is. Feel free to skip this section if you’re already familiar.

Industry observers note that baseline is a project from the WebDX Community Group that tells you, in plain terms, how safe a web feature is to use across the major browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari). A feature can be in one of three states:.

It has been revealed that that 30-month gap between “Newly” and “Widely” matters a lot for this audit. A feature that’s Widely available is something you can usually drop a library for today. A feature that’s only Newly available is something you can drop a library for if you check your audience first, or if you’re comfortable with a small feature check. We’ll treat those two cases differently throughout.

You can look any feature up on webstatus.dev, on MDN (every reference page reveals a Baseline badge near the top), or programmatically with the web-features npm package. We’ll use all three later when we run the audit on a real project.

It’s tempting to read “the browser does this now” and start ripping libraries out. Let’s not do that. A swap that looks free on paper can quietly break things for a chunk of your people, or cost you a feature you were relying on without realizing it.

In a recent development, so before dropping any library, ask three questions. We’ll reuse these in every cluster below.

1. Is the replacement Baseline-safe for my audience?

In a recent development, not “is it Baseline” in the abstract, but “is it safe for the people who actually use my app.” If the native feature is Widely available, this is usually a yes. If it’s only Newly available, check your analytics or your browserslist config and see what share of your users would miss out. A B2B dashboard where everyone’s on the latest browser is a very different situation from a public-facing site with a long tail of old Android devices.

2. What does the swap actually cost?

In a recent development, dropping a library isn’t always free. Sometimes the native feature isn’t supported widely enough yet, so you’d reach for a polyfill. If that polyfill is heavier than the library you’re removing, you’ve made your bundle bigger, unless you load it conditionally. We’ll see exactly this with Temporal later.

According to recent reports, 3. Does the platform feature cover my real use case?

Sources indicate that libraries often do more than the platform feature they resemble. axios isn’t just fetch with automatic JSON parsing; it has interceptors, request cancellation, and retries. If you’re using those, a straight swap to fetch will leave you reimplementing them. Check what you actually use before assuming it’s a drop-in replacement.

Keep these three in mind. Every cluster below is really just these questions applied to a different corner of your dependencies.

This is the cluster where you’ll usually find the most KBs sitting on top of features that are already Widely available. The browser ships a whole family of formatting tools under the Intl namespace, and a lot of small, popular libraries became unnecessary.

Here are the usual suspects and what replaces them:.

Let’s walk through some of them.

timeago.js exists to turn a timestamp into “3 hours ago”. Intl.RelativeTimeFormat does the same thing, and it’s Baseline Widely available.

It has been revealed that the numeric: "auto" option is the nice touch here: it gives you “yesterday” instead of “1 day ago” where the language has a word for it. You pass a number and a unit, and you get a localized string back.

In a recent development, you may be wondering about the one thing timeago.js does that this snippet doesn’t: it picks the unit for you. Given a date, timeago.js decides whether to say “seconds” or “days.” Intl.RelativeTimeFormat expects you to do that part. It’s a few lines of arithmetic (work out the difference, find the largest unit that fits), and once you’ve written that helper, you don’t need the library anymore.

Intl.NumberFormat covers most of what number-formatting libraries do: thousands separators, currency, percentages, and compact notation.

And Intl.ListFormat, Widely available, handles the “join an array into a sentence” problem, including the Oxford comma, which is the kind of thing people write fiddly helper functions for:.

Recent findings suggest that humanize-duration turns a number of milliseconds into “1 hour, 30 minutes”. The platform equivalent is Intl.DurationFormat:.

One thing to keep in mind is that Intl.DurationFormat is Baseline Newly available at the time of writing, not Widely available. It landed in all the major engines in March 2025, and it’s on track to become Widely available in 2027. So this one fails question 1 for broad-audience apps unless you check your traffic first or add a fallback. For an internal tool on modern browsers, it’s fine today. For a public site with old devices, give it another year or guard it with a feature check.

According to recent reports, if your app uses the full set (humanize-duration, timeago.js, pluralize, numeral), that’s roughly 14 KB gzipped of dependencies, most of it replaceable right now with Widely available APIs. The internationalization cluster is usually the easiest win in the whole audit.

This cluster is more nuanced, so it’s a good one to slow down on.

According to recent reports, the browser HTTP libraries people reach for are axios (17 KB gz) and superagent (19 KB gz). For most requests, fetch plus AbortController covers what you need, and both are Widely available.

According to recent reports, the one extra line (res.json()) is fetch being explicit where axios was implicit. That’s the pattern across this whole cluster: fetch does less for you by default, and you decide whether you want the things it leaves out.

axios has a timeout option. fetch has AbortSignal.timeout():.

This is where question 3 does most of the work, so let’s be specific about the gaps:.

Recent findings suggest that I personally heavily rely on interceptors in my interactive online courses, such as Learn JavaScript, and I have solved that for years using a custom class on top of fetch. I’ve shipped this to millions of users and have seen lots of success with it.

According to recent reports, none of these are hard to rebuild, and most apps only use one or two of them. But this is exactly the kind of cluster where you shouldn’t do a blind find-and-replace. Look at how you actually use your HTTP client first. If it’s plain GETs and POSTs, dropping axios for a thin fetch wrapper saves you about 17 KB gzipped.

This cluster has some of the most satisfying swaps, because the platform features don’t just match the libraries, they’re often more accessible than what teams ship by hand.

The libraries here are modal dialogs (something like a11y-dialog, 1.8 KB gz), tooltip and popover libraries (tippy.js, 14 KB gz, which bundles Popper for positioning), focus-trap (6.6 KB gz), and body-scroll-lock (1.3 KB gz). They get replaced by three platform features: the element, the Popover API, and CSS anchor positioning.

Sources indicate that A huge amount of modal-related code exists to solve accessibility problems: trapping focus inside the modal, closing on Escape, restoring focus to the previous element when the dialog is closed, and rendering above everything else. The element, Widely available, does all of that for you.

It has been revealed that calling showModal() does the work that focus-trap was installed for: focus moves into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert so you can’t tab out of it, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The dialog renders in the browser’s Top layer, so you don’t fight z-index. You also get a ::backdrop pseudo-element to style the overlay.

That single element can replace your modal library and focus-trap. The one piece it doesn’t handle on its own is locking the background from scrolling, which is what body-scroll-lock was for. That’s now one line of CSS:.

It has been revealed that if you’re wondering why we’re using dialog:modal instead of dialog[open], it’s because the open attribute is set as soon as you call show(), but the dialog isn’t actually modal so you don’t want to lock scrolling yet. The :modal pseudo-class is only true when the dialog is actually modal, which is the case when you call showModal().

So three libraries collapse into one element and one CSS rule.

For things that aren’t full modals (dropdown menus, tooltips, the small floating panels that tippy.js handles), the Popover API gives you light-dismiss behavior, top-layer rendering, and Escape-to-close with no JavaScript at all:.

Clicking the button toggles the popover. Clicking outside it closes it. It’s Baseline Newly available (since January 2025).

The other half of what a tooltip library does is positioning: keeping the floating element pinned to its trigger and flipping it when it would overflow the viewport. That’s what Popper (bundled inside tippy.js) handles, and it’s now a CSS feature called anchor positioning. Here it pins the same #menu popover directly under its trigger button:.

Industry observers note that anchor positioning is the newest feature in this article. It became Baseline Newly available in January 2026, when Firefox 147 shipped it (Chrome had it since version 125, and Safari since version 26). Because it’s this fresh, it’s squarely a question-1 feature: great for modern audiences, but check your traffic, and note that some of the more advanced parts (like position-try fallbacks) have uneven support across versions. Keep a sensible fallback for older browsers.

Between , the Popover API, and anchor positioning, the UI primitives cluster (tooltip library, modal library, focus-trap, body-scroll-lock) adds up to roughly 24 KB gzipped, and you come out the other side with better accessibility defaults than most hand-rolled solutions.

According to recent reports, lodash is rarely imported whole anymore, but its individual functions show up everywhere, either as the full lodash package (25 KB gz) or as standalone installs like lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby. Several of the most common ones now have direct platform equivalents.

Recent findings suggest that lodash.groupby reorganizes an array into an object keyed by some property. Object.groupBy does exactly that:.

There’s also Map.groupBy for when you want a Map instead of a plain object (handy if your keys aren’t strings). Both are Baseline Newly available, since March 2024, and on track to become Widely available in late 2026.

lodash.clonedeep makes a deep copy of an object. structuredClone is the platform version, and it’s Widely available:.

structuredClone handles the tricky cases that trip up JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...)): it clones Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, and circular references correctly. The limit to know about (question 3 again) is that it can’t clone functions, DOM nodes, or class instances; it throws on functions and drops the prototype on class instances. For plain data, which is what most people deep-clone, it’s a clean replacement.

If you’ve ever pulled in a Lodash helper for union, intersection, or difference, the Set object now has these built in. They’re Baseline Newly available, since June 2024:.

The full set of methods is union, intersection, difference, symmetricDifference, isSubsetOf, isSupersetOf, and isDisjointFrom.

Sources indicate that not all of Lodash has moved into the platform. debounce and throttle still have no native equivalent, and they’re genuinely useful, so cherry-picking lodash.debounce is reasonable. The point of this cluster isn’t “delete Lodash,” it’s “stop shipping the parts the browser already has.” Dropping lodash.clonedeep and lodash.groupby alone is about 8 KB gzipped, and if you were importing the full lodash for a handful of functions, replacing the platform-covered ones can let you drop it entirely.

Every cluster so far has ended in “go ahead, drop it.” This one is the opposite, and that’s why it’s worth including: it shows the framework telling you to wait.

Temporal is the long-awaited replacement for JavaScript’s Date, and it’s a genuinely better API: immutable objects, sane time zone handling, and no more month indexes starting at zero. It reached TC39 Stage 4 in March 2026 and is part of the ES2026 specification. Firefox shipped it in version 139 (in 2025), and Chrome shipped it in version 144 (January 2026). Safari hasn’t shipped it in a stable release yet; it’s in Safari Technology Preview, with stable support expected later in 2026.

If Temporal is news to you, check out the Temporal Cheatsheet for a quick overview of the API and a comparison to Date.

However, Temporal is not Baseline. It’s still in limited availability, because Safari people don’t have it. To use it across all browsers today, you need a polyfill, and this is where the math turns against you.

The official @js-temporal/polyfill is about 44 KB gzipped. There’s a smaller polyfill that internally does not depend on BigInt and it weighs 19 KB gzipped. A lightweight date library like dayjs is about 3 KB gzipped. So if you swap dayjs for Temporal plus its polyfill right now, you’re not saving 3 KB, you’re adding roughly 41 KB to your bundle, unless you are able to load the polyfill conditionally.

According to recent reports, the verdict is generally clear: keep dayjs (or date-fns) for now. The moment to revisit is when Safari ships Temporal in a stable release and it reaches Baseline. At that point you can use Temporal natively and conditionally load the polyfill for customers on older browsers. This is a feature to write down and check again in a few months, not one to act on today.

It has been revealed that the clusters above are a starting map, but your dependencies are your own. Here’s a repeatable process you can run this quarter.

Start by listing what actually ships to owners:.

Industry observers note that for a quick per-package number, Bundlephobia gives you the minified and gzipped size of any npm package. For the real picture (what each dependency costs in your actual bundle, after tree-shaking and deduplication), run a bundle analyzer against your build. npx source-map-explorer works on most bundles, and npx vite-bundle-visualizer works for Vite projects.

For each candidate, find the platform feature that would replace it and check its Baseline status. The quickest way is webstatus.dev or the Baseline badge on the feature’s MDN page.

It has been revealed that for each library with a platform replacement, go back to the framework: Is it Baseline-safe for your audience? What does the swap cost? Does the feature cover how you actually use the library? Most of your decisions will fall out of question 1 (check the feature’s status against your browserslist) and question 3 (check your own usage).

For Widely available features, swap and move on. For Newly available ones, either confirm your audience is on modern browsers or guard the upcoming code with a quick feature check and keep a fallback:.

That way you ship less code to the users who can run it, without breaking the ones who can’t.

It has been revealed that add the clusters up, and the picture is concrete. The internationalization cluster is around 14 KB gzipped, HTTP is around 17 KB, the UI primitives are around 24 KB, and the Lodash utilities are 8 KB or more depending on how much of the library you were shipping. For a typical mid-sized app, that’s somewhere between 60 KB and 90 KB gzipped of dependencies you can hand back to the platform, and more if you were shipping the full lodash or several of these libraries at once. (The uncompressed numbers are two to three times larger, which is what you’ll see in a bundle analyzer before gzip.).

According to recent reports, I’ve chosen relatively lean packages for most of these features, but some individual packages could still be heavy. Your dialog package, for instance, could alone weigh as much as 50KB gzipped depending on what you’re using.

A few features are worth keeping an eye on over the next year, because they’ll open up further swaps:.

Recent findings suggest that none of this is a one-time cleanup. The platform ships new features constantly, and the gap between “you need a library for this” and “the browser does this” keeps closing. The habit worth building is small: once a quarter, run the audit. List your dependencies, check what’s now Baseline, and hand back what you can.

Pick one cluster from this article, open your package.json, and see how much of it the browser already does for you.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server.
  • MongoDB, the firm that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.
  • Industry observers note that the affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A critical flaw in MongoDB Server allows an unauthenticated attacker to send two requests that trigger a crash on the database server. The crash occurs only if that server is later chosen to take over as the main server while it still lacks some recent changes.

MongoDB, the firm that makes the database, released fixed versions earlier this week.

Industry observers note that the affected servers are members of a replica set, a group of MongoDB servers that keep copies of the same data. One member, the primary, serves as the main server and handles all newly introduced writes, while the others replicate them. If the primary becomes unavailable, the other members hold an election to pick a new primary.

Sources indicate that researchers at Datadog Security Labs reproduced the crash in a lab and published their findings yesterday. On vulnerable versions, turning on authentication does not stop the two requests. An attacker cannot make the targeted member fall behind or win an election, or see when either happens, the researchers said.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, is a use-after-free: the server ends up using memory it has already freed. MongoDB rated it 9.5 out of 10 on the CVSS 4.0 severity scale. The company said it found the flaw itself and was "not aware of any attempts to take advantage of this vulnerability.".

Affected members include the shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod, a single server outside any replica set, is not affected.

Each affected branch has a fixed release, listed below and in the CVE record. Every earlier version in a branch is affected, back to the branch's first release.

MongoDB Atlas clusters automatically receive fixed versions during maintenance, the company stated in its security announcement. Customers who defer maintenance should apply the upgrade as soon as possible.

Self-managed deployments need the fixed release on every replica set member. After upgrading, check the version each member is running, including members in containers and any that were offline during maintenance.

In a recent development, the 8.2 branch is not among the affected versions listed, and its newest release is 8.2.12. But a proof of concept published on GitHub reports that 8.2.12 still exhibited the bug in a lab test using a test-only setting.

It has been revealed that the 8.2 branch reached end of life on July 31, according to the company's lifecycle schedule. Past that date, a version no longer receives fixes, including security fixes.

Until a member can be upgraded, the researchers advise restricting network access to the database to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the two requests but does not fix the flaw.

In a recent development, A member who wins an election first catches up by applying the writes it missed before it accepts fresh ones. The flaw is in the cleanup that runs when this catch-up step ends, according to the Datadog researchers' technical analysis.

The two requests are ping commands that carry a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each asks the server to wait until replication reaches a certain point, and the server records a pending notification for it, called a waiter.

It has been revealed that planting the waiters does not crash the server. They do not expire, and stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back or steps down from primary.

It has been revealed that the crash needs the member who received the requests to win a later election, even though it is behind another member. When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice, reusing memory that was already freed, and the upcoming primary crashes before it accepts any writes. Once those conditions are met, the crash does not depend on winning a timing race, the researchers said.

Sources indicate that in the lab, the researchers caused the member to fall behind and forced a failover themselves by using admin access to pause and stop mongod processes. Only the two requests came from a client without credentials, and that client could not write to the database.

On version 8.0.34, the member crashed with a segmentation fault, leaving the lab cluster without a primary. Another deployment might elect a fresh primary and keep running.

Industry observers note that in the fixed version 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as unauthorized at once, and the member kept running. One part of the fix lets only system users use readConcern.afterOpTime.

MongoDB indicates the flaw may also result in arbitrary code execution in the server process under certain conditions. In the lab, though, "we did not achieve code execution," the researchers said. Their results also do not show how often the attack would work in other setups.

The proof-of-concept code reproduces the bug in a lab replica set, according to its author. Its reliable mode requires a test-only setting that a remote attacker cannot enable. Its stated impact is a crash or memory corruption, with no claim of code execution.

The second part of the fix stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters are already in place, the researchers noted. They did not test that part themselves.

In the proof-of-concept lab test, which ran with authentication turned off, the fixed 8.0.37 accepted the planted waiters but ran the cleanup only once.

To look for planting or a crash, check the server's structured logs for these signs from the researchers' vulnerable run:.

According to recent reports, A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not point to this flaw. The requests may also arrive before the failover, so check earlier logs from the same member too.

Whether the request fields are logged depends on logging settings, and the attr.remote field may show a loopback address instead of the client's real IP.

When front-end developers and UX engineers are tasked with building a web interface that feels tactile, bouncy, or destructive, the industry instinct is almost always the same: reach for a physics engine. Frameworks like Matter.js, Cannon.js, or custom WebGL solutions have become the gold standard for creating immersive, gamified websites.

Industry observers note that when our team at Isadora Agency set out to build Stress Release, a digital stress-relief squeeze toy designed to let burnt-out creatives smash, stretch, and distort animated UI characters, we initially explored that route. The goal was to build a highly tactile experience where every click yielded a satisfying, squishy reaction.

But as we began prototyping, we realized something crucial: Physics engines produce plausible motion, but in our case, the animators produced intentional motion.

We didn’t need our characters to act like realistic rubber balls bouncing uncontrollably around a canvas. We needed them to react in very specific, highly designed ways. So, we scrapped the physics engine entirely.

In this article, we’ll break down how we built a real-time stress-relief squeeze toy without a single line of WebGL or Matter.js, relying entirely on programmatic Lottie state controls, DOM manipulation, and distance-based math.

Sources indicate that our core requirement for Stress Release was absolute deterministic control. Our animators had crafted bespoke .json Lottie files that required exact, frame-by-frame sequencing.

Recent findings suggest that for instance, our ‘mega squeeze’ reaction required a precise 181-frame build-up followed by a specific release sequence. To honor this design, we needed an architecture that wouldn’t overwrite the animators’ crafted keyframes with algorithmic approximations.

The tighter the click-feedback loop (click → squish → score), the more you need deterministic frame control. By choosing programmatic state control using Lottie’s native API, we ensured that the interaction layer acted as a flawless trigger for the animation layer.

According to recent reports, because our architecture relied on Lottie and the standard DOM, rendering is handled directly by the Lottie runtime, which plays the JSON-based vector animations as SVGs internally. We selected elements directly by ID and CSS class, driving their behavior using a combination of Lottie animation segments, CSS transforms, and click-event math.

To achieve a deeply satisfying “tactile feel” upon hitting a character, we used radial input mapping. The first step was converting the click from page coordinates into the character’s local coordinate space.

Every click was measured against the character’s center point, then translated into score, feedback intensity, and explosion placement:.

Then we calculate the straight-line distance from the center of the click using the Pythagorean theorem:.

That single number drives everything: the score, the feedback intensity, and where the explosion animation appears:.

The result is a concentric zone system — a perfect circle of scoring rings around the character’s center, similar to a dartboard. The visual complexity of the Lottie SVG is completely irrelevant to hit detection; the hitbox is always a clean circle. Critically, the explosion Lottie animation is repositioned to (a, b) — the same vector used for scoring, so it always appears exactly where the player clicked. This spatial accuracy creates the tactile “I hit that” sensation entirely through math and DOM positioning.

Industry observers note that because the experience used DOM-managed SVG elements, desktop clicks and mobile taps could be handled directly through native event listeners. This avoided extra raycasting or coordinate remapping layers, while keeping the interaction model aligned with how the animations were rendered.

Sources indicate that since the game requires a visual reaction at a specific point, Lottie handles all the squish and bounce feelings internally through its animation curves. Each character has a defined set of animation sections (idle loops, reaction frames, and end states) stored as frame ranges. When a click lands, we jump directly to the exact segment that matches the current game state:.

On every click, we advance through the play order and fire the next segment:.

When the segment completes, control returns to the idle loop:.

And for the mega squeeze build-up, the bar loops on a specific frame range until triggered:.

Sources indicate that another major factor in our architectural decision was responsive behavior. Because we built Stress Release in the DOM, we bypassed the complexities of scaling bounding boxes and collision vectors across different devices.

We handled responsive resizing entirely through CSS variables. By recalculating CSS custom properties on every resize, the layout simply reacts to the updated variables, and the Lottie SVGs scale naturally inside their containers without losing their state:.

While this architecture gave us total control over the art direction, it introduced a different challenge: file size.

Lottie JSON files can be heavy. We had 21 different character animations, plus multiple explosion variants that all needed to load. To ensure the experience remained fluid — especially on mobile devices — we implemented a few aggressive optimization strategies:.

When determining the stack for a gamified web experience, it is critical to let the design requirements dictate the technology.

Because our interactions required bespoke, highly controlled visual reactions, we opted for programmatic state control over emergent simulation. This decision empowered the animators to dictate the exact feel of the experience, leaving the code to do what it does best: listen, calculate, and trigger.

By mapping Lottie’s native timeline capabilities to the DOM, you can deliver incredibly rich, tactile user experiences while maintaining absolute control over the art direction.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate owners.
  • According to recent reports, the Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire.
  • Recent findings suggest that the messages show up as Google Calendar invites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, since mid-August 2026, a phishing operation has been stealing live Google sessions from corporate owners. Every check defenders normally lean on to judge a link came back clean, and the operator designed it that way on purpose.

According to recent reports, the Threat Research team at Material Security spotted the campaign and has since taken down hundreds of attacker domains in an effort the team calls Operation CloudFire. Here’s what the researchers found.

Recent findings suggest that the messages show up as Google Calendar invites. Some arrive by BCC, and many come from an organization the recipient has already traded email with. The pretexts are deliberately boring: voicemail notifications, RFP and RFI requests, court summonses, and missed payment notices. Nothing about them stands out in a busy inbox.

Sources indicate that most of the links point to Google itself. The usual pattern runs through Google’s own /url redirector, with the real destination tucked into a query parameter. Other waves used share.google and Drive file links the same way, and one variant leaned on Intuit transaction notification links. Whenever a message gets scored, the domain, certificate, and reputation on display are all legitimate.

Once a victim clicks through, the attacker runs a live reverse proxy in front of the real Google sign-in page. The victim types a password, gets a genuine prompt, and approves it while the operator watches in real time. The server passes each second factor along to Google as it comes in, whether that’s an SMS code, an authenticator code, Google’s Tap-Yes number matching, or phone-based account recovery. None of those controls stop the session from being captured.

The framework behind it, known as Nyasher, has been publicly documented since February, after researchers found a hardcoded key in its JavaScript.

According to recent reports, reputation systems answer questions about ownership. They ask who registered a domain, what else it has hosted, and whether anyone has complained about it. This campaign was built so every one of those answers came back harmless.

Recent findings suggest that it works in three layers. The first is Google’s redirector, which gives the initial hop a trusted Google URL. The second is a Cloudflare Turnstile challenge, and in some builds it’s the real widget served from Cloudflare’s own infrastructure. The third is the password capture page, and that’s where things get tricky for defenders. There’s no static site to scan. JavaScript builds the page in the browser after the visitor clears the challenge, so a crawler has nothing to fetch and a proxy log has nothing to record. As far as the researchers know, nobody had scanned those pages before the campaign was documented.

It has been revealed that the infrastructure is also meant to be thrown away. Early waves used many lure domains spread across several registrars, and most were registered just days before use. Receiving endpoints went live one to twenty days ahead of the wave they served. One wildcard certificate was issued 46 minutes before the domain it covers was even registered. Blocking any single piece costs the operator a few dollars and an afternoon.

Researchers tracked the campaign from the start, following each variant as lures, gates, and endpoints rotated. Once detections were in place, they caught more than 99% of the malicious messages, with a reclassification rate of 0.01%. It’s been steady work, since the attacker kept changing tactics, themes, and lure text to slip past static, machine learning, and agentic detections.

According to recent reports, what worked was refusing to let any one signal make the call. Reputation alone wouldn’t have caught this. Neither would link analysis, since the first hop is a Google URL and the final page doesn’t exist until a browser builds it. Instead, the detection approach weighs technical indicators alongside the apparent intent of the message, where its links actually end up, and the sending relationship behind it. Any one of those can be enough to act on. A detection built around a single signal inherits that signal’s blind spots, and this operator has put real effort into mapping them.

Sources indicate that where the analysis happens matters too. Gateways built to inspect mail in transit aren’t a great fit for calendar invites, and much of this campaign arrives as invites. Calendar invites need to be treated as a threat surface of their own, with the account’s full history used as context next to the technical signals.

In a recent development, A hijacked session leaves its trail in Google Workspace audit logs. A live session reaches mail, Drive, and the ability to grant OAuth access in the victim’s name, so the blast radius goes well past the inbox.

Recent findings suggest that that raises a couple of hard questions for security teams. Who’s actually reviewing those audit logs, and how fast can they act on what they find? Could the team revoke sessions, contain OAuth grants, and reset the affected account within an hour? Plenty of programs can’t, and an attacker holding a live session can do a lot in an hour.

By late September, the researchers decided that tuning rules, retraining models, and updating agents wouldn’t solve this alone. Detection protects customers, but it does nothing about an operator who’s already prepping the next wave. So the team went after the infrastructure.

Analysts pulled the gateway and backend URLs as messages were being sent and reported them through Cloudflare’s abuse reporting system. Cloudflare’s abuse team confirmed the fake interstitial and the proxied Google sign-in page behind it, then put its own phishing warning in front of those destinations.

That had two effects. First, the attacker’s infrastructure got burned. Every reported gateway and endpoint had to be re-registered, re-pointed, and re-certified before the operator could send again. Second, it protected people well beyond any one tech giant’s customers. Anyone who clicked a reported link saw a warning page instead of a credential form.

Recent findings suggest that these figures only cover organizations that agreed to share data, so the real totals are higher. Over one month of Operation CloudFire, researchers recorded:.

The messages also followed a clear rhythm, with sends tracking US business hours.

The sender count explains how the campaign earned trust. The attacker controlled each compromised account before the first invite went out, and each one sent invites to the account owner’s saved contacts, among others. Recipients saw a name or domain they knew, on a domain with a clean history, at a sensible time of day. Reputation feeds had no reason to flag any of it.

It has been revealed that the phishing themes have moved from calendar invites to Google Drive file and document share invites. Researchers haven’t seen a matching jump in other lures or tactics, and activity from this group seems to have scattered. For now, the campaign looks finished.

According to recent reports, that’s a snapshot, and it could change fast. Rebuilding the infrastructure is cheap, and the framework has been public since February. The operator also shipped an unfinished Microsoft 365 branch alongside the live Google code. It includes a stylesheet path, a second harness, and a title string that decodes to a Microsoft sign-in prompt. None of those paths resolve today, and adding the new brand would only mean dropping in a file, with no code changes. The follow-on is built and waiting.

The researchers see the theme rotation as ongoing iteration and expect the next pivot to look a lot like this one, just with a different brand on it.

Recent findings suggest that the full technical breakdown, including indicators of compromise and a timeline, is in the companion whitepaper. Teams hunting for this activity in their own environments should start there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that there’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping new AI rules” in the EU. In reality, it’s a lot more narrow — and a lot more sensible. And mostly it’s about making AI more obvious when it actually needs to be obvious — especially for AI-generated content.

In a recent development, starting from Aug 2, 2026, AI labelling is a legal requirement for any manufacturer that serves EU citizens. And similar to European Accessibility Act, it’s not limited to EU companies. It affects any company worldwide with EU operations as long as their AI output is used by people in the EU. Let’s see what exactly it means for us.

The goal of AI labelling is to help everyone exposed to AI content to recognize, in a clear and distinguishable way, that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

According to Article 50(4) of the AI Act, AI labelling applies to:.

It has been revealed that both providers (who build or supply the AI system) and deployers (who use it) carry legal obligations. Similar to GDPR and EAA, a firm doesn’t escape Article 50 just because it licensed an external AI tool from a third party.

However, it doesn’t mean that all AI-generated content must be explicitly labelled.

Beyond the use cases above, pretty much everything else — the vast majority of AI-assisted work — simply isn’t covered by fresh transparency rules. Most notably, the disclosure obligation does not apply where the AI-generated text has been reviewed and edited by a human, with a named person or entity taking editorial responsibility for it.

Some confusion circles around what exactly “public interest” means, where it starts and where it ends. On its own, it refers to health, safety, environment, economy, finances, politics, science, or culture. If AI-generated product claims touch upon them, the disclosure rule applies.

It has been revealed that some law firms recommend labelling realistic AI-generated illustrations or photos as a precaution for advertising, marketing and other commercial content. AI-generated product illustrations, photos, or posters do need a disclosure, as long as they resemble a real person, place, object, or event.

But at which point does edited AI content stop being AI content? When a form is pre-filled with AI, but then a user edits it, is it still AI? EU Commission’s guidance is a little fuzzy. Small assistive edits — spellcheck, grammar, formatting, cropping, colour correction, and AI-generated translation — don’t count as AI generation.

AI-generated summaries, composite imagery, substantive rewrites, or adding and removing elements from a photo are considered AI generation. In practice, fine-tuning a sentence a person wrote is fine, but generating the sentence on its own requires a disclosure.

“A human skimmed it before publishing” doesn’t qualify as editorial review. The Commission is explicit that it needs to be substantive, with a named person responsible for the editorial control.

In other words, the fine line lies between intentional manual intervention and automated generation. The latter always has to be disclosed (exception: closed B2B environments).

As part of the Code of Practice, the European Commission has published an EU AI icon set. It’s a specific “AI” mark (similar to the AI label in Carbon Design System) — not the generic ✨ sparkle that many products use to signal AI. The signal must be “clear and distinguishable”.

The sparkle might be too ambiguous to signal AI clearly. Mostly because it’s often used to mean “AI-powered feature”, rather than “this specific content was generated by AI”. That’s the kind of signal EU guidelines are trying to rule out.

The Commission is explicit: using an icon “does not establish legal compliance by itself.” A barely visible icon, a note buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second are all not compliant.

Recent findings suggest that the icon should be clearly visible, with a plain language label and accessible to assistive technologies. A safe bet is to pair any icon with plain text (“AI-generated”) — and it needs to persist when being reshared or downloaded.

In fact, the EU Commission also published Code of Practice on marking and labelling of AI content.

It might feel like a yet another regulation coming from the EU, but in reality there are plenty of other similar regulations that emerged recently worldwide:.

Industry observers note that all of these are signs of upcoming AI regulation that looks more like a pattern, rather than a coincidence. So if you’re shipping anything AI this year, it’s probably a good idea to have a conversation about what exactly is going to be AI-labelled, and what not.

One final note is that upcoming EU AI transparency rules are much broader than US laws on AI disclosure, where certain state laws require disclosures for synthetic human performers, political advertising or specific AI applications.

Sources indicate that none of this really deserves panic or confusion. It’s about a fairly simple idea that has been emerging worldwide at almost the same time:.

If anything, it will help people distinguish between AI slop and not AI — and everybody can only benefit from that.

N-able on Thursday said it's investigating a latest public disclosure containing claims of additional vulnerabilities in on-premise versions of N-central running version 2026.4.1 HF2.

"Based on our initial review, the server matter described depends on a non-default configuration in which the Legacy API is turned on and exposed to the public internet," N-able remarked in a new advisory. "Legacy API is turned off by default in the product and is not recommended.".

The company is urging customers to disable Legacy API immediately, if not already. It also noted that hosted environments are not affected by this concern.

The incident impacts the following services -.

The development comes days after N-able released 2026.4.1.26 to address a number of security flaws disclosed by independent security researcher Sean Bales earlier this week. The vulnerabilities are collectively tracked under the name Able2Shell.

The latest shortcoming, also revealed by Bales, have been codenamed 4EverAble2Shell and Agent2Shell, adding the proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits successfully work against N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), the enhancement N-able released on November 10, 2026, to resolve Able2Shell.

According to the researcher, 4EverAble2Shell enables unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on N-central servers. Agent2Shell, on the other hand, leverages more than 10 zero-day vulnerabilities to run commands on managed Windows agents as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, assuming the attacker knows the target appliance ID.

It has been revealed that ryan Dewhurst, founder and CEO of Previdian, told The Hacker News that targeted N-central probing has been observed against 4EverAble2Shell within hours following the release of the PoC. The activity has originated from the IP address 157.20.241[.]16. There is no evidence of successful exploitation as of writing.

In the attack chain observed by the threat intelligence manufacturer, threat actors have been observed attempting to achieve initial code execution through a recently disclosed Apache Axis flaw (CVE-2026-90436, CVSS score: 9.8), followed by attempts to escalate privileges to root using 4EverAble2Shell, and then download and execute a shell script from 157.20.241[.]16 using curl.

Dewhurst noted the development marks the first documented instance of exploitation attempts aimed at CVE-2026-90436, patches for which were released on November 6, 2026.

In a post shared on X, watchTowr also mentioned it's seeing probes for 4EverAble2Shell targeting N-Central builds with the Legacy API enabled.

Sources indicate that we know that everything on the web is a box by default, but you’ll find many animated s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real , you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble wearing HTML/CSS can. has a strict no .html policy.

The tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

Besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

It has been revealed that if you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to proposal an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated swiftly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:.

It has been revealed that that’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can quickly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a newly introduced animation, let’s initiative all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

It has been revealed that I like to initiative my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

For now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:.

See the Pen [colorAndOpacityChange [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016dc-399c-7652-b172-4cd4663746b9) by Johan Grobler.

It has been revealed that the important thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

According to recent reports, A big part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

Let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

Industry observers note that using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

See the Pen [syncbase.end [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/emgwwGJ) by Johan Grobler.

Sources indicate that something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

See the Pen [syncbase.begin [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/xbgooXq) by Johan Grobler.

Syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

Recent findings suggest that let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:.

Recent findings suggest that browsers have wide support for the prefers-reduced-motion media feature and Val Head explains this in depth in another article. We definitely want to respect this user preference as we consider moving things around. In fact, consider it non-negotiable.

Recent findings suggest that there are various approaches to adhering to a user’s prefers-reduced-motion setting when it comes to SMIL. Each with its pros and cons. Evaluating early on what’s going to work best for your use case could save you a partial rewrite down the line.

For example, we could consider using a element instead of a plain because supports multiple elements that can be used as fallbacks in a media attribute for reduced motion preferences.

Sources indicate that or one SVG file with an inline CSS @media query that uses display: none to swap between versions. That mentioned, it’s an approach that might cause trouble in various environments. But browsers are continuously changing, and this might not be an concern in the future.

You might also consider a CSS background-image instead because we can wrap that style in a media query — @media (prefers-reduced-motion) — that sets a static image as the fallback for reduced motion preferences.

There are even more options we can turn to! For example, SVG’s element can also be used to swap things out for motion preferences.

Or, if we prefer everything bundled together, we can use JavaScript .matchMedia() and the handy SMIL DOM interface to control which animations start instead of completely switching out files.

For this, I’m avoiding any motion and sticking to opacity animations, which tend to cause less trouble. For a non-interactive animation like this, we can load it in an tag. When we add motion, we can go the route to show the most appropriate version of our animation.

We’re going to do our own version of the classic three-dot spinner:.

It has been revealed that SVG wizards might be able to do everything directly in a text editor. I recommend using a graphic editor like Inkscape if you’re having trouble visualizing how the markup will be rendered. Once again, Andy Clarke has a great article about his process for optimizing and structuring his own drawings.

Note: There’s a gotcha with Inkscape. Setting what you would expect to be an element’s ID via the Layers window actually sets the value of a metadata attribute used internally by Inkscape. Use Inkscape’s object properties or XML editor window to set the true element’s ID. Your mileage may vary with a different editor. Also, in Inkscape, remember to save the file as optimized SVG when the drawing is done to strip away unneeded metadata.

Our naming scheme is going to be straightforward: we’ll call them #fadeIn and #fadeOut, and to differentiate between each pair of tags, we’ll postfix the tag’s ID with either Left, Middle or Right. Try to follow a convention that makes sense to you when coming up with your own IDs.

To narrow our choices a bit, all of the tags will use the same dur value, and none of the syncbase values will have offsets.

For someone coming from a culture that reads from left to right, the dots appearing on screen along the same pattern would feel natural. Let’s also start with all the dots fading out together at the end:.

Later, if we want to move the fade-outs in time, all we do is change when #fadeOutLeft starts.

Industry observers note that as you iterate on your animation, timing charts are a great way to keep track of your work, and they make visual comparison between versions possible. And by drawing a timing chart, you might even see a pattern in the timing between the parts of the animations that you might otherwise have missed.

Recent findings suggest that as you animate more elements and properties, it gets harder to keep track of what starts when. To see how timing charts can help you make sense of things, let’s build on the basic spinner:.

See the Pen [staticDotsWithClipPaths [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/01a016f4-f99c-7779-b526-1265ecf5619b) by Johan Grobler.

We only need a single for all three dots, but it adds structure to the document, and it’s good practice to wrap it, and similar tags, in a tag:.

Industry observers note that remember to set the clip path for the s. Either with CSS or using the clip-path attribute:.

That’s all the changes the graphics need. Have a look at the animated version with its timing chart, then we’ll look in more detail at the changes that have been made to the animation:.

There’s a new animation, #moveClipPathLeft, that starts the whole sequence, and to tweak the animation’s rhythm a bit, there’s a 1s delay between when the fade-outs end and the loop restarts:.

You could use s to move the rectangles instead, but we need to move them back to their starting positions at the end for a smooth restart of the animation. You’ll need to take into account which tags can animate and set which data types if you do decide to animate the transform attribute instead of translating the rectangles with the y attribute.

To change things up, the for the middle dot moves down:.

We’re also using the fill-opacity property instead of the opacity property for the fade-ins, and they’ve been synchronized to start once a dot’s clipping has finished moving:.

The fade-outs still use the normal opacity property, so both the fill and stroke fade out together. Because this arrangement is set up to use a group fade-out at the end, there are a few places the markup could be optimized. One of them is dropping the fill="freeze" to automatically reset the dot’s opacity back to its starting value once the tag finishes running:.

In a recent development, for the tags that did use fill="freeze", we’ll use tags to reset those properties back to their starting values. I’ve simplified the chart a little by lumping those tags together. Because these tags don’t have a duration over which they act, on the chart I’ve drawn the start and end markers over each other.

To reset the fill-opacity on the left dot:.

If you use fill="freeze" with the fade-outs, you’ll need an extra for each dot to reset the middle dot’s opacity:.

Sources indicate that the last thing we need to do is move the clipping rectangles back to their starting positions. For the right :.

Industry observers note that that’s just one of the possible timing variations, and most of what you’ll need to try some of the others, as we did with the basic spinner, is already in place. You might want to have a try at coming up with a couple of your own alternate timings.

In a recent development, to sum things up, we know that balancing the different stages of an animation can be difficult at best, and untenable at worst. Any time we get into multi-step animations that exceed one or two steps, it’s a form of orchestration. You’re almost building a Rube Goldberg machine of markup. And using a timing chart is a strategy I use that I hope will help you in your projects as well. They are outlines of what to expect and when, allowing you to map things out in a way that not only helps plan your code, but also makes future updates and maintenance a lot more bearable than going into it without a plan.

While a timing chart can’t reduce the complexity of the markup, it can give a good overview of what should happen when. Timing charts are definitely not limited to SMIL animations. Unfortunately, syncbase values are, and they can still help even if you’re going to use a different approach to implementing your animation.

I highly recommend checking out Andy’s other articles on Smashing Magazine. There’s even more stuff on combining CSS and SVG.

Yosra Emad wrote a great article on creating animations with multiple steps in CSS, and you might want to try drawing a few timing charts as you read through it.

When you’re ready to start adding those in-between lines to your timing chart, Nash Vail’s article on easing dives deep into the details of easing curves.

You might also be interested in tests for your browser’s SVG implementation to see what is supported.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Cloud Moves the Compute Engine API to Immutable Date-Based Versions.

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.

Google Cloud has made multi-versioning of the Compute Engine API generally available, adding immutable, date-stamped API versions beside the long-lived /v1 surface. Stable versions are named YYYY-MM-DD and released quarterly, starting with 2026-09-01; preview versions carry a -preview suffix and a one-year lifespan. A caller selects one with the X-Goog-Api-Version header or the $apiVersion query parameter on the unchanged /compute/v1/ path, and a request that names no version keeps getting /v1, which has no end-of-life date.

Recent findings suggest that software engineer Michael Murstein writes that the problem was the shape of /v1 itself. Because it "was a single, mutable production surface shared by every customer worldwide," any behavioral improvement, "even changing a counter-intuitive default or modernizing an error format," risked breaking existing scripts or required a multi-year migration. Google calls the replacement interface-based versioning, aligned with its own AIP-185, which requires stable versions to be dates and previews to be time-bound. Each stable version is a locked snapshot of all generally available features and defaults at that date, and no breaking change is made to it after publication.

The blog post names three differences a caller will notice:.

Most callers will meet the change through tooling rather than headers. Each client library release for Python, Go, Java, Node.js, C#, Ruby and PHP now binds to one date-based version while keeping the compute_v1 and apiv1 namespaces, so no import paths change, and -preview SDK releases carry the preview versions. gcloud compute targets the bundled stable version and a new gcloud preview compute group targets the bundled preview, with existing compute, beta and alpha scripts unchanged. The Terraform google provider targets stable versions and google-beta targets preview, with no version setting in HCL. Discovery documents are published per version.

In a recent development, with this release, Google is the last of the three largest cloud providers to let callers pin an API version on a request. Azure Resource Manager has required a date-stamped api-version query parameter, with a -preview suffix for previews, since its REST API debuted, while AWS keeps date-stamped service models inside its SDKs and does not expose version selection on a request. The header form Google chose is the one Stripe popularized outside the cloud market; its Stripe-Version header now takes values such as 2026-10-28.endive, with monthly releases that carry no breaking changes and a major release twice a year that may. Google's quarterly cadence sits between Azure's per-service dates and Stripe's monthly ones, and unlike Stripe it has not remarked which quarterly versions will carry breaking changes relative to the previous one.

Google gives no end-of-life date for /v1, no path by which a preview version becomes stable, no complete list of behavioral differences between /v1 and 2026-09-01 beyond the examples above, and no statement on whether other Google Cloud APIs will adopt the scheme; the /beta and /alpha channels are not mentioned. Both 2026-09-01 and 2026-10-01-previews are available in all regions today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Cloud VMs on AMD Turin chips need a guest OS patch and a stop-and-start to protect against three CPU side-channel flaws, Google mentioned this week.

Sources indicate that the company has already applied mitigations against attacks between VMs, and between VMs and the host. Inside a VM, the flaws may let an attacker with code on the same processor core infer data from other processes or the kernel.

Sources indicate that the affected machine series are C4D, N4D, H4D, Z4D,, and G4, including bare-metal instances of C4D and Z4D. Turin is the code name for fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors.

All three flaws are Transient Scheduler Attacks (TSA). Two of them, TSA-SQ (CVE-2024-36350) and TSA-L1 (CVE-2024-36357), were first disclosed on July 8, 2025, for earlier EPYC processors.

Sources indicate that AMD now indicates its Zen 5 processors, which include Turin, are "impacted differently from previously characterized AMD processors." The third flaw, CVE-2026-0004, is new. It may let an attacker who can run code on a system infer data in the processor's L1 data cache.

Industry observers note that the Xen Project, which maintains the Xen hypervisor, calls the new flaw TSA-Fill. It also claims an earlier statement has been corrected: "AMD had previously mentioned that Zen5 CPUs were not vulnerable to TSA-SQ and TSA-L1.".

Google rates the issue Medium. AMD classifies all three as local attacks with high attack complexity that require only low privileges, according to its Zen 5 bulletin and CVE-2026-0004 advisory.

As of today, none of the three is in the KEV catalog of exploited flaws kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Neither company reports any exploitation in its bulletins.

Google's security bulletin gives these steps for each service:.

Customers on older Rome, Milan, and Genoa processors got the same stop-and-start instruction in an earlier bulletin at the time of the original disclosure on July 8, 2025.

Recent findings suggest that the company lists nothing to do in the meantime for VMs whose OS vendor has not yet shipped a fix. It also does not say how to tell when the CPU information update has reached a VM.

Sources indicate that A kernel commit that mitigates TSA on Zen 5, including the fresh variant, is in the Linux kernel source tree. As of today, Debian has fixed CVE-2026-0004 in its Linux kernel only in its unstable branch. Its security tracker still lists the kernels in bookworm, trixie, and forky as vulnerable.

Industry observers note that for Turin servers on your own hardware, AMD says both platform firmware and OS updates are needed to mitigate the flaws fully. The mitigation may affect performance, and administrators should weigh the risk to their own workloads, according to its technical guidance.

Sources indicate that the Xen Project has published hypervisor patches in its Xen advisory. It says microcode for all TSA flaws on Zen 5 has been in linux-firmware since September 23.

Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pierre Burgy is the co-founder and CEO of Strapi, the leading open-source headless CMS, and co-founder of Fimo, a product incubated at Strapi that keeps … More about Pierre ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
