#107. Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2050 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine

Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

📅 2026-10-16 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • According to recent reports, the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that paul is a leader in conversion rate optimisation and user experience design thinking. He has over 25 years experience working with clients such as Doctors … More about Paul ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

According to recent reports, the way I see most organizations roll out AI feels more like a farce than a strategy. If it were turned into a movie, reviewers would say it was unbelievable. Nobody could be that stupid.

Yet here we are. And what makes it all the more frustrating is that we have been here before.

Back in 2014, I wrote a book for Smashing Magazine called Digital Adaptation, looking at the mistakes being made in how organizations were approaching digital transformation and what they should be doing instead. The similarities between then and now are striking.

So in this post, I want to look back at Digital Adaptation and see how the lessons in that book apply to the AI era and what we can learn from the past to help us navigate the challenges of AI today.

The biggest mistake, both then and now, is approaching each as a technological challenge.

Sure, both digital transformation and AI are technological advances, and yes, some level of technological implementation is required. But that is the tip of a very large iceberg.

According to recent reports, back in the midst of the digital transformation era, IT departments were rolling out CMSs, CRM systems, intranets, and so on. Meanwhile, on the customer-facing side, organizations were rolling out websites, apps, and personalization. But they were putting almost no emphasis on how people were going to use these systems.

Internal systems were hard to use, and customers either didn’t care what was being built or wanted something else entirely.

The same is happening with AI. Senior management are buying into the hype, and IT teams are rolling out Copilot Studio licenses company-wide and considering the job done. Sure, there is a bit of organization-wide generic training, but that’s about it.

Just like before, staff are left wondering what to do with these new systems and feeling under pressure to use them and deliver results.

After all, this time around, it is even worse, because this time, staff fear for their jobs. They have read the same headlines that you have, and no amount of promises from senior management is going to make them feel any better.

According to recent reports, I mean, think about it from a staff member’s point of view. AI offers them very little personally, even setting aside the fact that management may be intending to use it to replace them.

The main reason senior management are excited about AI is that it provides additional productivity. People can do more in less time. But that does not benefit staff. They are still required to work 9 to 5, but now they are expected to do more in the same time. They don’t get any time back, and they don’t get paid more, so why would they embrace AI?

Recent findings suggest that one strategy is to help staff identify the parts of their job they hate and how AI can help them do those tasks more quickly and less painfully. People tend to be a lot more receptive to change when it is presented as an opportunity to improve their working lives.

According to recent reports, but, that should just be the beginning. Organizations may need to consider providing incentives for staff to adopt AI in terms of career progression, compensation, or shorter working hours.

Also, adopting AI is not a simple task. It involves challenging every working practice they have built up over (in some cases) decades. All of that procedural knowledge has to be rebuilt. That is a lot to ask of anybody in even the best of circumstances, and most employees do not find themselves in the best of circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that most are overworked and struggling to stay on top of their to-do lists. They don’t have time to sit down, learn a new tool, and figure out how it fits into their workflow.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t just take time. It also takes a lot of consideration and experimentation. It is not enough to just send a member of staff on a training course and expect them to be able to use AI to its full potential.

Sources indicate that at a minimum, staff need training specific to their roles, such as the AI training I provide to UX teams. But organizations should be going even further.

According to recent reports, they need to develop sophisticated training programs that help staff from different departments understand how to use AI in their specific roles. They need ongoing support and the time to experiment with AI to find the best ways to use it.

It has been revealed that but formal training will only take you so far. In my experience, the most effective support comes from colleagues, which is why I would start with the enthusiasts rather than the resisters. Every organization has a handful of people who are already experimenting with AI, often without anybody asking them to. Bring those people together, give them the time and space to share what is working for them, and let their enthusiasm spread to everyone else.

I saw this work during the digital transformation era too. In Digital Adaptation, I described an internal conference where staff revealed their colleagues what they had built, and it did more for adoption than any memo from the top ever could. People are far more likely to try something when they see a colleague in a similar role using it successfully than when they are told to by senior management.

Unfortunately, experimentation comes with a substantial downside… mistakes will be made.

Many organizations have, to be frank, a culture of fear where mistakes are seen as a sign of incompetence. However, by its very nature, learning a latest tool like AI will involve making mistakes, and this can be a massive barrier to adoption.

Sources indicate that I saw this during the era of digital transformation. Senior management would demand digital transformation and were confused when it didn’t happen.

It has been revealed that what they didn’t realize was that they were sending mixed messages to staff. Sure, they were asking for digital transformation, but they were still demanding that the same key performance indicators (KPIs) be met, and they still pointed out any mistakes in their annual reviews.

There was no space to fail, as the pressure to deliver was relentless.

In a recent development, this time around, it seems to be even worse. I hear horror stories of staff being reprimanded for using too many tokens just weeks after being told to adopt AI. Or staff being lectured so much about what they should or should not do with AI that they are afraid to try anything. It is safer to just do what they have always done.

Look, I get it. AI cannot be rolled out without some governance in place, but again, this is an area that organizations have typically handled poorly.

In the midst of digital transformation, governance would either be non-existent, or it would be so strict that it would stifle innovation, and unfortunately, I see the same pattern emerging with AI adoption.

Industry observers note that staff need some governance to help them know where they stand. It helps them understand what is expected of them and what they can and cannot do.

In a recent development, but too often organizations have been so strict that it is easier not to do anything at all. Pages of instructions about what people should and should not share with AI create that sense of fear that I mentioned earlier.

Of course, mistakes will get made, but that is the cost of change, and so organizations need to accept that and do what they can to mitigate that in how they roll out the technology.

Recent findings suggest that that stated, organizations will need to be careful in how they roll out AI from an IT perspective. Once again, it is easy to lock everything down and stifle the adoption of AI.

It has been revealed that again, this is something I highlighted back in 2014 with digital transformation. Overstretched IT teams would pick a set of technologies and roll them out organization-wide, often with little or no consultation with the individuals who would be using them. Anything outside of that set of technologies had to go through a complex approval process, normally involving a steering committee. The result was a glacial pace of change that was one of the major contributing factors to the failure rate of digital transformation projects.

Today we are seeing the same thing. IT teams are opting into a tool like Copilot and calling it a day, but that often falls massively short.

Take, for example, a UX team I am working with at the moment. Management is pushing hard for AI adoption, and the team is excited about the potential of creating an AI-powered research repository and even AI personas. It sounds like a wonderful case study in AI adoption, with enthusiastic management, an excited team, and innovative ideas.

Unfortunately, the reality is that nothing is happening because Copilot cannot deliver on the team’s vision, and so they are presently bogged down in bureaucracy as they try to persuade the AI steering group that they need to use a different toolset. Understandably, the team’s enthusiasm is waning. Why bother?

And that team is one of the more patient ones. In many organizations, staff are not waiting for the steering group at all. Just as we saw shadow IT during the digital transformation era, with people signing up for Dropbox and Google Docs because the official tools could not do what they needed, we are now seeing shadow AI. When the in-house AI tool will not let people do their jobs, they open a personal ChatGPT or Claude account on their phone or home laptop and get on with it.

That is far more dangerous than the problem the restrictions were meant to prevent. Manufacturer data ends up in tools the organization has no control over, with no oversight and no record of what has been shared. In trying to lock everything down, organizations end up pushing the risk somewhere they cannot see it.

Sources indicate that the instinctive reaction is to clamp down with stricter policies, blocked websites, and warnings about disciplinary action. But that rarely works, and it drives the behavior further underground. Shadow AI is a symptom, and a useful one, because it indicates exactly where the official tools are falling short.

Look, I understand the cost of a messy, out-of-control tech stack. It is not ideal. However, in the early days of adoption, we may have to live with a bit of chaos while people explore the edges of what is possible and work out common use cases.

Organizations need to allow staff to explore different uses of AI and even different AI apps to find what suits their specific needs in their specific roles. They can always start locking things down later as the real organizational needs become clearer.

I admit all of this feels dangerous to some organizations. They want to control the AI adoption process centrally and make sure nothing goes wrong. I understand that. But change comes with a degree of risk, and the risk of moving too slowly is greater than the risk of moving too fast.

However, a bigger danger still is when organizations see this as a technological challenge and overlook the human side of things. AI adoption is not simply about rolling out new technology. Just like digital transformation, it is about people, culture, and change management. The sooner organizations realize the scope of what they are dealing with, the better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unknown threat actor has been observed targeting unpatched Check Point Security Gateways to obtain initial access via the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities and then a previously unreported local privilege escalation flaw in Gaia OS  to deploy a backdoor called TSGA.

The activity, detailed by Check Point, began on October 30, 2026, and targeted Israeli organizations, with a broader follow-up wave on November 2, 2026, that targeted organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Some of the organizations singled out in the first wave have also been at the receiving end of destructive actions that include the deployment of wiper malware.

Recent findings suggest that "PHP2Shell provided initial access, followed by privilege escalation through the DynamicCLI interface, tracked as CVE-2026-123039," Check Point noted. "The attackers then deployed PHP web shells, the persistent TSGA backdoor, and its embedded TSProxy networking component.".

"The attackers pivoted from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt notes during the destructive stage.".

CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS score: 7.8) is a missing authorization flaw that could enable privilege escalation to root in the DynamicCLI process, enabling any authenticated local user to run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to the socket.

"The issue is a local privilege escalation and requires the attacker to already have local code execution on the appliance," Check Point mentioned, adding it "observed an active exploit of this vulnerability against a couple of dozen customers.".

The concern impacts versions R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10, and R81 of the following products -.

"In late October 2026, approximately one week after a security fix became available, activity originating from 130.94.19[.]204 targeted Israeli organizations through vulnerable Mobile Access portals on Check Point Security Gateways," Check Point mentioned.

"Evidence suggested some cases of a successful compromise, with exploitation activity consistent with PHP2Shell, associated with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.".

In a recent development, after obtaining initial access, the unknown hacking group is mentioned to have escalated privileges from the portal service account to root by weaponizing CVE-2026-123039 and deploying PHP web shells with an aim to establish persistent access. The web shells support command execution and file upload capabilities.

The November 2, 2026, wave is noted to have targeted some Israeli organizations that had already been targeted in the first wave, alongside other organizations worldwide, without demonstrating any specific geographic or sector preference, indicating an opportunistic initial-access effort.

Recent findings suggest that the access afforded by the web shell paves the way for TSGA, a standalone passive backdoor that also includes a second component called TSProxy. TSGA, deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon, has been described as a Linux gateway implant with Check Point-specific functionality, offering encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering.

In a recent development, "[TSProxy's] injection code loads this library into selected appliance processes, where it intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while allowing ordinary traffic to continue," Check Point noted. "This combines a persistent standalone backdoor with concealed access through existing appliance services.".

Some of the other post-exploitation actions observed are listed below -.

Both TSGA and TSProxy are assessed to be Check Point-specific components of a toolkit dubbed PhiliKit that was first documented by ESET in  June 2026, attributing it to a China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221).

Other factors that point to the involvement of a possible China-aligned threat actor include the use of LightNode VPS infrastructure and the fact that scanning activity was concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC, coinciding with typical Chinese working hours.

However, the cybersecurity firm remarked it does not have enough evidence to link the latest campaign to the threat actor or other known Chinese-nexus groups, citing the following reasons -.

"Taken together, the evidence does not allow us to assess with high confidence the true nature of this operation," Check Point noted. "Several scenarios remain plausible: the identified actor ran the entire campaign, acted solely as an initial access broker, or took part in a false-flag operation. It is also possible that the destructive activity served as a smoke screen.".

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, on November 13, 2026, added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the patch by November 16, 2026.

OSNMA and Galileo HAS on a real autopilot: what you can switch on today, and how to verify it

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we are UAV GNSS (uav-gnss.com), a Septentrio-powered receiver maker.
  • Spoofing is not a noisy signal — it is a clean one that lies.
  • In a recent development, if you only buy anti-jamming you are still open to a good spoofer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we are UAV GNSS (uav-gnss.com), a Septentrio-powered receiver maker. Most integrators we talk to confuse two different jobs: proving the position is real and making the position accurate without a base station. Galileo's OSNMA and HAS are two separate answers to those two questions, and both are now switchable on a normal autopilot build without touching the flight controller. Here is what each one actually does, what it cannot do, and how to see it working in your logs.

Spoofing is not a noisy signal — it is a clean one that lies. A spoofed receiver typically reports excellent C/N0, a healthy satellite count and a fixed-looking solution, because the receiver has no reason to doubt the data. Jamming is the opposite: the signal is bad and obvious.

In a recent development, if you only buy anti-jamming you are still open to a good spoofer. If you only buy authentication you still lose the solution in RF noise. They are separate line items.

OSNMA (Open Service Navigation Message Authentication) is Galileo's free, subscription-less authentication service. The constellation broadcasts a cryptographic signature chain alongside the navigation data, and a receiver with OSNMA support verifies it before trusting the satellites. A transmitter that did not come from the Galileo control segment cannot produce a valid signature, so a spoofer can imitate the ranging signal but not the authentication.

Recent findings suggest that what it does not do: it authenticates Galileo only. GPS, GLONASS and BeiDou are not covered. On a multi-constellation receiver, that means a partial solution can still be authenticated while the rest is not, which is why you must look at which satellites are authenticated, not just whether the flag notes "yes".

Septentrio's mosaic-X5 and mosaic-G5 have OSNMA integrated (see our page on anti-spoofing for drones for the receiver-side detail). In practice you configure it with a three-way mode, and the mode you pick is the whole design decision:.

Strict is what most people actually want for security, but it costs you satellites and it needs a disciplined clock (the driver documentation puts the OSNMA firmware floor at GNSS firmware 4.12.1, with strict operation depending on host time sync). On a vehicle with no NTP, "loose + flag monitoring" is the honest configuration — and then you have to route those flags somewhere an operator sees.

Sources indicate that if you run ROS, the official Septentrio driver publishes the authentication status as its own topic (/galauthstatus) next to /aimplusstatus and /rfstatus, so authentication state is observable in rqt or recorded in a bag like any other signal. That is the difference between "OSNMA is enabled" and "I can prove the solution was authentic at t=142 s".

Industry observers note that HAS (High Accuracy Service) attacks the correction problem instead. Galileo broadcasts free precise corrections two ways: signal-in-space on E6-B at 1278.75 MHz (448 bit/s per satellite, no internet needed), or over the internet via the IDD stream. The receiver applies them internally and outputs a better position over the same serial/Ethernet stream your autopilot already parses.

In a recent development, the official target is under 20 cm horizontal, and in our own measurements on a mosaic-G5 P3H module we have seen around 10 cm class results; the detail is in our HAS explainer. Three honest caveats:.

This is the part that surprises people. Both features live inside the receiver. The autopilot continues to receive the same SBF/NMEA stream at the same baud rate with the same GPS_TYPE it already uses — no newly introduced parameters, no new message definitions to parse. The difference highlights up in the quality of what arrives, and in the status flags you choose to monitor.

Sources indicate that that last row is the one worth scheduling before a customer demo. Enable strict mode, feed a simulator a trajectory that walks away from truth, and confirm the receiver's solution does not follow it. If you have never run that test, you do not know whether OSNMA is doing anything.

Wiring, parameter tables and the SBF stream checker are in our integration repo: github.com/uavgnss6-bot/septentrio-gnss-integration-guide.

Question for the room: if you run OSNMA today, are you in loose or strict mode — and what made you choose it? We are collecting real configurations, especially from builds without a disciplined clock on the host.

We’re back! Don’t worry, this isn’t a trick (despite what our name suggests!). However, due to the hiatus, we’re also a little behind. That’s why this concern of What’s !notable is absolutely stacked. All killer, no filler. Here’s what you missed.

In a recent development, by the way, before we dive in, Mat Marquis’ highly recommended JavaScript for Everyone course is currently -30% off (code: CSSTRICKSFRIENDS). You don’t want to miss this.

Industry observers note that preethi Sam demonstrated how to create background image refraction effects with CSS. The effects are stunning, can be animated, don’t need very much CSS (no JavaScript), and we don’t need to duplicate the image either.

Brecht De Ruyte demonstrated how to build customizable components using container style queries and advanced attr(), showcasing some incredible interactive demos, including the two below:.

Sources indicate that dan Holloran highlighted us how to use the different scroll-state() queries (scrollable, scrolled, snapped, and stuck). It’s not a long read, which is exactly what you want for a fresh but simple feature like this.

A quick, no-context CSS snippet to entice you:.

In a recent development, declan Chidlow shared some of the craziest CSS to ever exist, and I mean craziest. Most of it comes from Internet Explorer, but let’s face it, you knew that already. Thankfully, they don’t build them like they used to.

Bramus demonstrated how to animate CSS grids using anchor positioning. The idea is that we anchor content to its corresponding cell, and then as the grid reflows, it’s the content (not the cell) that animates with it.

(But it doesn’t work in Firefox due to what sounds like a bug.).

According to recent reports, chris Coyier talked about a bunch of new HTML features, and honestly, there’s a whole lot in there that you definitely haven’t heard of. Like, I’m certain of it.

Recent findings suggest that victor Ayomipo contemplated why container query adoption has been so terrible despite them topping CSS wishlists for years. Victor thinks that we’re using them wrong, so he’s here to set the record straight.

Cory LaViska demonstrated how to use @custom-media in addition to container style queries as a fallback.

Also, don’t forget that Declan has an extremely thorough @custom-media deep-dive in our Almanac.

Industry observers note that ahmad Shadeed tackled an interesting topic — detecting overlapping elements (with CSS, of course). If you’re keen on anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations, and again (!), container style queries, then this walkthrough is for you.

I want to know when the decorative element hits the section from the left edge, taking into consideration that the element might have a fluid position or size that changes with the viewport size or container size. Basically, it’s a dynamic problem. It’s not about using a media query to hide the decorative element, I want to hide it upon overlapping.

Maybe container queries are finally picking up?

Industry observers note that patrick Brosset walked us through a proposal for the previewsrc HTML attribute, which would enable us to supply preview images for images that haven’t yet loaded using only HTML. For example, we could supply a blurry preview image. However, I’d rather have something like :loaded/:not(:loaded) so that we can style/transition unloaded images with CSS rather than needing to create extra images.

Temani Afif shared a custom borders demo, where the trick is to declare a transparent border, use border-shape to define its shape, then declare a background in addition to background-clip: border-area so that it only indicates up within the border, like this (requires Chrome at the moment):.

In a similar manner, Leon Arnott shared this awesome trick for animating the background color of ::selection, something that’s actually forbidden (or so we thought, anyway…):.

Industry observers note that today in CSS: We all know you can change the highlight colour of selected text, but it's impossible to animate that colour. Unless… the colour was just a variable inherited from the parent element, using @​property to make it animatable… Hahahahaha… [image or embed].

According to recent reports, and that’s it, really. Simply use var(--bg-color) on ::selection or some other visually restrictive element.

Chris Coyier demonstrated how to random()ly animate an element along the edge of another element. There’s a cute doggo, by the way. Probably should’ve led with that.

Polypane explained how we might disable the root scroller accidentally (which is surprisingly easy to do — I’ve definitely done it), what we lose in doing so, and what to do instead.

Also, have you ever completely misunderstood how the root (:root/html) works? This is a solid explainer for that, too.

Speaking of accidents, have you ever tapped on a target twice, apparently in quick succession, and ended up zooming in? Andy Bell revealed that touch-action: manipulation disables the double-tap-to-zoom-in functionality. It isn’t upcoming, but I don’t see many web developers using it. One for the CSS reset, I think?

Chrome and Firefox now ship every two weeks. The inaugural releases were fairly exciting (not smaller, as I assumed they’d be). In addition, Safari 27 (along with iOS, iPadOS, and macOS 27) shipped with some of the same features as Firefox, making them Baseline in the same release window. High fives all around!

And, as always, thanks for tuning in!

#101. Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2181 w)

Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

📅 2026-10-20 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brecht De Ruyte is a self-taught front-end developer located in Belgium with a passion for UX and Design. After more than a decade of working in tech, he … More about Brecht ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In design, we love spending hours obsessing over consistency, grids, and alignment. But when I heard that the native CSS random() function landed in Safari and is rolling out in Chrome 156, I started wondering: where does randomness actually make sense on the web? Is it something we want in our design system? To find out, I did what I always do in doubt: I built a bunch of playful CodePen demos exploring organic typography, bouncing letters, splayed cards, and a punk fanzine.

As someone who loves building design systems and tinkering with CSS architecture, a big part of my day job revolves around control. We set up spacing scales, lock down typography, set up color tokens, and make sure everything aligns on a grid. Consistency is usually our bread and butter as design engineers and a proud badge of skill when creating design systems. If a card suddenly jumps 20 pixels to the left on a refresh, it’s not creative expression; it’s a bug that the project manager will log.

So when I first heard that the native random() function from the CSS Values and Units Level 5 spec was shipped in Safari, and is at the moment rolling out in Chrome 156 (with positive signals from Mozilla on Firefox as well), my first reaction was: that’s pretty cool!

And my second reaction was: wait… where would I actually use this without making a mess? How can I convince designers that random might be a good idea for a design system?

Because let’s be honest: why on earth would we want randomness in our stylesheets when we’ve spent the last decade trying to make the web more predictable? Even when using flexbox or fluid typography, we’re still trying to make things as aligned and uniform as possible.

If you step away from the browser for a second and look at physical things around you, nothing is ever truly uniform.

According to recent reports, take an old letterpress print: the ink bleeds slightly into the paper grain, some letters have a microscopic tilt, and the baseline isn’t always that straight. Or think about a deck of Polaroid photos dropped on a coffee table; those photos aren’t perfect, probably not straight either. Or what about lights flickering in a street at night? That little bit of analog messiness is what makes things feel alive, organic, and human.

On the web, we’ve gotten so good at pixel perfection that sometimes our interfaces end up feeling a bit sterile. We notice this even more now with rapidly created designs by an unguided LLM; we usually end up with the same sort of design we had 10 years ago. Everything is squared off, aligned, neat. It works, but frankly, it does get a bit boring.

Recent findings suggest that randomness in CSS doesn’t have to mean throwing your design system out the window. It’s about little imperfections and playfulness. Maybe let’s even call it fun.

Industry observers note that to see what this actually looks like in practice, I spent a few hours tinkering in CodePen. The demos might feel a bit isolated, but I’m sure that many designers could make the best of this controlled chaos. But before we look at those demos, let’s take a look at the syntax.

Recent findings suggest that the random() function is specified in CSS Values and Units Module Level 5. It generates a pseudo-random value inside your CSS without needing JavaScript or a build-time Sass loop.

The formal specification looks like this:.

In practice, and across current browser implementations, you can just write comma-separated arguments:.

It won’t be a shocker for most people, but I thought I should at least mention that your minimum and maximum bounds must share the exact same unit type.

The CSS parser needs to know what dimension it’s dealing with. You can use lengths, angles, time, percentages, or plain unitless numbers:.

If you ever need to combine units, you’ll have to reach for calc() inside the arguments so each side resolves properly.

In a recent development, the optional third argument is the step size. If you don’t add it, the browser picks from a continuous range. But if you provide a step, it rounds the random value to discrete increments:.

This can be helpful in cases where you want things to jump around a bit, but you still want them to land on your pre-defined grid.

It has been revealed that normally, every time random() is evaluated on a property, it creates an independent random value. But there could be an example where you create a box that sets inline-size and block-size at random, but at the same time you need them to match so the element stays a perfect square.

That’s where the caching key comes in:.

In the latest spec, a bare dashed ident like --square-size shares its seed globally across every element in the document (which would make all cards identical). To keep width and height linked on a single element while giving each card its own independent size, the spec requires pairing it with the element-scoped keyword (e.g. --square-size element-scoped).

Recent findings suggest that to see this in action, I created a little example. In the top row, the tiles have uncached dimensions, which distorts each tile into an unpredictable, mismatched rectangle. In the bottom row, both inline-size and block-size share --square-size, guaranteeing that each tile remains a pristine 1:1 square. Refresh the CodePen a couple of times and notice the bottom cards keeping the same randomness:.

See the Pen [Uncached vs cached random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e91-4bac-765e-b04e-a53636759163) by @utilitybend.

Because we’re still in the rollout phase, you’ll want to wrap your experiments in @supports:.

Industry observers note that there’s also another function in the spec called random-item(). While random() handles numerical ranges, random-item() lets you pick from a list of predefined tokens or keywords:.

This can be handy to randomise from a set of design tokens. This one does not have any browser support at the moment, but it certainly is something to look forward to.

And now for the practical part.

It has been revealed that when I started playing with the feature, I was also doing some typography tricks with animations. So that’s where my first thought went: Typography! What if we just add a tiny bit of imperfection to a word?

Think of vintage book covers. The letters aren’t misaligned by miles, but they have small imperfections.

See the Pen [Imperfection random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-157f-708d-a704-fa067114aaca) by @utilitybend.

Here is the CSS powering the letters:.

I also added a little hover effect. While you’re reading, the word feels playful. But the second you hover over it, every character snaps back.

Recent findings suggest that one quick accessibility warning here: If you break a word into separate elements so you can style each letter, screen readers will often read it out as individual characters: “i - m - p - e - r - f - e - c - t - i - o - n”, or pause awkwardly between each one. That’s a terrible user experience.

Always hide the visual spans from assistive tech and provide the full word:.

Screen reader consumers get the clean text, and sighted users get the fun visual quirks.

Once I had those letters sitting there with their little tilts, I couldn’t resist: what if we animated it?

Industry observers note that I started tinkering with a bounce keyframe. I was just goofing around, but the end result gave me a little smile. If you animate every letter with the exact same timing, you get that clean sine wave we’ve all seen before. But if every letter gets its own jump height, its own duration, and its own landing squash, suddenly the word looks like a bunch of little characters jumping around on a trampoline.

See the Pen [Bouncy imperfection with CSS random() [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e92-c117-729f-9844-ddf19fc1fc96) by @utilitybend.

Here is how the bounce parameters are wired up:.

Notice the negative animation delay (--delay: random(-3s, 0s)).

Recent findings suggest that if you set a positive delay, the letters sit frozen on page load, waiting for their timers to expire before jumping. By using a negative delay, the browser pretends the animation has already been running for a few seconds. The moment the page loads, every letter is already bouncing at its own rhythm.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve built cards. Lots of cards. So many cards… Portfolio grids, blog summaries, feature lists. And most of the time, they sit in three or four neat, boring columns.

For dashboards, that’s exactly what you want. But if you’re building a lifestyle portfolio, a children’s website, or a collection of vacation photos, we can be a bit more playful. In the following example, I did just that:.

See the Pen [Random card tilt [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e93-849d-72a9-9254-3f4305e58a34) by @utilitybend.

Here’s how I put that together:.

In the example, playing around with the shadow was a fun experiment. I will probably try more effects with that in the future.

Sources indicate that here is where modern CSS features start getting really interesting. In the previous demo with tilting cards, we used pure randomness. But what if you have a stack of cards that needs to fan out across the screen as you scroll?

In this example, I decided to use math for the structure and randomness for the human imperfection.

See the Pen [Scroll drivin animations with random() tilted cards [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e94-79c6-70b1-97d4-66b7c2d736b0) by @utilitybend.

Look at how cleanly this works:.

If you’ve ever looked at brutalist or high-end fashion websites, you’ve probably seen horizontal marquee text drifting across the screen as you scroll down the page.

Usually, you see developers creating classes like .drift-slow, .drift-fast, .drift-reverse, or using a hefty JavaScript scroll listener to compute transforms.

With random() and a tiny bit of math, we can get procedural drift speeds in just a few lines:.

See the Pen [Random() velocity scroll animation [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-4cbe-77bd-9128-685d2c75cc56) by @utilitybend.

calc(pow(-1, sibling-index())) gives us alternating directions (1, -1, 1, -1), and random(15%, 44%) decides how fast each row travels. As you scroll, each typographic line moves at its own tempo.

It has been revealed that I love photography, and one of my favorite things about prime lenses is shallow depth of field. When you shoot at a wide aperture like f/1.7, only whatever is right on your focal plane stays sharp. Everything else melts away into soft bokeh. Yep, photography is all about that bokeh!

By combining random() with filter: blur(), opacity, and scale, we can recreate that lens feel:.

See the Pen [All about that random() bokeh [forked]](https://codepen.io/editor/smashingmag/pen/01a15e95-fe50-76dc-943b-d75fcaf704e6) by @utilitybend.

In a recent development, some words land at blur(0px) with full opacity right in front of your eyes. Others blur out to 6px or 8px and fade into the background. And when you hover over any blurry item in the back, it rack-focuses right into sharpness. It’s a great little effect for decorative hero sections or tag clouds.

Now that we’ve played with the wild side, let’s talk about where this actually belongs in our daily work.

But! I am happy to be proven wrong here. I encourage you to challenge the status quo and experiment with this.

Any time you use animations, you have to respect user preferences for reduced motion:.

In a recent development, if someone prefers reduced motion, it could also be a good idea to flatten the angles, not just the animations. I can imagine that a lot of random angles can also upset people while scrolling. Design should be fun, but never at the cost of accessibility.

Tinkering with random() over the last couple of days was a lot of fun. I’m still not sure if I’ll be able to convince my designer friends, but what I do know is that it brings a bit of joy.

Sources indicate that whenever we wanted a bit of organic randomness on the web, we had to make compromises: either pull in a JavaScript animation library, or write huge preprocessor loops that spit out hundreds of lines of static CSS. Having this built into the browser engine with zero JavaScript overhead is such a welcome addition.

We spent the last decade mastering consistency, tokens, and design systems. Now that we have that foundation in place, maybe it’s time to let a little bit of playful messiness back onto the web.

I really believe that the web is supposed to be fun.

Never mind the defaults; here is CSS random().

#99. Operation Endgame Takes Down Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC Servers, Seizes 6.4M Stolen Logins

Operation Endgame Takes Down Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC Servers, Seizes 6.4M Stolen Logins

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An international police operation took down servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC this week.
  • Police also seized about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims, according to Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).
  • Gootloader is a loader: once on a computer, it could download other malware, especially ransomware.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An international police operation took down servers behind Gootloader, CastleRAT and StealC this week. Criminals used the three malware tools to gain access to computers, steal passwords, and launch ransomware attacks.

Police also seized about 6.4 million stolen logins belonging to more than 40,000 victims, according to Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

Gootloader is a loader: once on a computer, it could download other malware, especially ransomware. It spread through fake legal documents placed on hacked websites, often WordPress sites. Criminals used SEO poisoning to push those sites high in search results.

According to recent reports, gootloader has infected at least 25,000 computers worldwide since 2018, the U.S. Justice Department remarked. Its operators used those computers to infect more computers, then sold access to the new ones to ransomware criminals. In the U.S., Gootloader was used in ransomware attacks against at least 44 victims, resulting in about $28.8 million in losses.

It has been revealed that german police gave a much higher count in their statement in German. Based on what investigators know so far, Gootloader has infected millions of computers worldwide since it first appeared in 2020.

It has been revealed that across the three tools, police seized 235 servers and 257 domains, according to an operation summary from Europol, which supported the action. The takedown is part of Operation Endgame, an international police campaign against malware criminals use to access victims' computers.

For Gootloader, police took down 14 servers and 218 domains and removed malware from 681 hacked websites.

In a recent development, with court approval, U.S. agencies and their international partners removed Gootloader from more than 100 servers, including hacked WordPress sites. They also seized U.S. domains used to deliver and control the malware, according to the Justice Department announcement.

It has been revealed that castleRAT, a remote access trojan (RAT) known since 2025, allows attackers to control an infected computer remotely. Police seized 120 of its servers and 39 domains.

StealC is an infostealer that exfiltrates passwords and other login credentials from infected computers, allowing criminals to sell or misuse them. Police took down its servers again this week, after a June operation against it.

Industry observers note that after that June action, its operators changed their infrastructure and brought it back online to stay out of investigators' reach, German police said. Some of StealC's key infrastructure ran on Virtualine/Omegatech, a bulletproof hosting service that advertised its services to criminals.

Police shut that hosting service down in a late-October takedown.

It has been revealed that no arrests were confirmed in this week's action. Dutch police also carried out further investigations targeting Gootloader's main suspect, according to their news release.

Dutch police have loaded data stolen by CastleRAT into Check your hack, a police service where people can enter an email address. If the address is in the data, the police send an email within a few minutes with steps to remove the malware. If it is not, no email arrives.

It has been revealed that more data will be added in the coming weeks. The service checks single addresses, not whole domains, but organizations can join No More Leaks, a police project that shares data with private partners. The stolen data is also being shared with services including Have I Been Pwned and the Shadowserver Foundation.

In a recent development, emails that claim to come from the police and ask people to check the data are fake. The police never send emails with links.

Sources indicate that even after police seize the data, criminals may still have the stolen logins, the police say in their frequently asked questions. As long as the malware stays on a computer, criminals may also keep getting its passwords.

The Shadowserver Foundation is working with internet service providers and computer security incident response teams (CSIRTs) to find infected computers and notify their owners, the Justice Department remarked. In Germany, the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) is helping notify victims, according to the BKA.

Denmark's National Special Crime Unit (NSK) helped clean the 681 websites. In a statement in Danish, the unit mentioned it believes the attackers got into the sites with stolen passwords that came through criminal channels. They then installed a backdoor.

Officers removed the attackers' code and access, and left a message for the site owners with advice on securing their sites.

Police in Denmark and the Netherlands advise WordPress site owners to take these steps, several of which are set out in a Dutch advice sheet:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything.
  • Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?
  • Recent findings suggest that for example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Something wicked this way comes.”.

It was naivety, but when I first came across Flexbox, and then CSS Grid, I had this feeling all those positioning properties (align-self, justify-content…) would be available to use on block and inline elements; things like tables, lists, fixed elements, everything. The workings might be different under the hood, depending on the reference boxes, but the syntax and expected outcomes would be same: push to one edge, keep at the center, spread around evenly, etc.

Although that didn’t happen, what if I made something of that sort?

Recent findings suggest that for example, I could take out the soul of an HTML table and stitch it back together with CSS Grid. In other words, it reads like a table, but acts like a grid, allowing me to use grid properties. Believe it or not, some form of this was used in the past to make tables responsive.

Before I kill off a table in this article though: there are a lot of advantages to straight-up tables. They provide a clean semantic layout that browsers perfectly understand and translate for assistive technology when needed. There’s even a element.

In a recent development, on the CSS side of things, there are indeed circumstances where CSS Grid is necessary for its intrinsic responsiveness, source order independence, and positioning. That’s why it’s an indispensable tool for layouts. Use that and let HTML tables to do the work of actually displaying tabular data!

In a recent development, but there’s the presentational benefit of table we should consider. Technically, is not a presentational element like a . It’s semantic: the browser and I share a common meaning for it. But whether the browser understands it as such or not, if I read I believe it’s a heading followed by data. Let’s say that’s pseudo-semantic to me, if presentation is not the right term.

That pseudo-semanticism is still useful. It’s the difference between me having to read this:.

Despite there being semantic elements for titles, like and , they don’t bring in the connection that and have, and it’s better to reserve and for textual structuring like glossaries rather than layouts.

According to recent reports, so, is it okay if I use this way? I mean, the table itself merely used as pseudo-semantic markup skin:.

Then, this CSS and its outcome (for the first markup):.

…changes to this (for the table markup):.

To me, the latter markup example — a pseudo-semantic table — is easier to scan than a handful of generic divs. I get the pseudo-semantics of table, and the ease of using CSS Grid for the layout. As for browsers, none of them have shunned this sort of Frankenstein creation, at least yet. The VoiceOver and keyboard navigation works as if it’s a real table.

But it’s understandable why it looks more than a little gross and against the grain of what we should be able to. We’re encouraged to maintain a separation of concerns between content and presentation and this does exactly that without affecting the tables semantics, such as its role. But maybe it should? There are plenty of other HTML elements that CSS is capable of busting.

So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Well, research indicates that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, owners expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a new page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Industry observers note that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

Recent findings suggest that the rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Industry observers note that using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a fresh page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

Sources indicate that it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow users to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

It has been revealed that for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

It has been revealed that the safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

In a recent development, but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — highlights all options and allows owners to drill down.

According to recent reports, and if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

#93. SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users

SilentAir Hijacks Asian Telecom Networks to Intercept SMS 2FA Codes and Spy on Taiwanese Users

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.
  • In a recent development, enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software organization based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week.
  • The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly identified spying group used hacked equipment inside Asian mobile operators to intercept the calls and texts of selected people, mostly in Taiwan.

In a recent development, enea, a telecom and cybersecurity software organization based in Stockholm, found the group's attack sources in at least six Asian countries and named it SilentAir this week. It assessed with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor, but linked its activity to China only with low confidence.

The company has told the operators where it found SilentAir sources. It said SilentAir has been disrupted for now but could return. The report does not say whether those operators have cleaned up the hacked equipment.

According to recent reports, mobile operators use the SS7 and Diameter protocols to exchange signaling messages that route calls and texts and enable roaming. This traffic crosses a shared network called the IPX, which runs on a high level of trust between operators. SilentAir sent its attacks into the IPX from the hacked equipment.

Recent findings suggest that for interception, SilentAir sent the target's home network an UpdateLocation message, or its Diameter equivalent. The message claimed that the hacked equipment was now serving the target's phone. If the home network accepted it, calls and texts for that person would be diverted to the attackers.

It has been revealed that some of these attacks worked. For some targets, the company observed two-factor authentication (2FA) codes being intercepted immediately after the diversion took effect. That points to an attempt to break into other accounts registered to those people.

The report gives no similar evidence for voice calls, and it does not say whether any account was taken over.

Interception made up 18.3% of the attacks the organization saw from SilentAir. For a typical surveillance company, the kind of firm behind most signaling attacks, the share was 2.1% in the company's earlier research.

Some targets were political and government VIPs in their own countries. In rare cases, SilentAir equipment in several countries worked together against such targets, which the manufacturer said points to a single controller.

Outside Taiwan, targets were mostly in other Southeast and East Asian networks, and at times in East Africa, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. People using the hacked operators' own networks may also have been targeted, but the tech giant could not see that traffic.

The organization spotted SilentAir by studying attacks on the links between operators. Since early 2025, it has tracked unusual attacks, mostly over SS7 and sometimes Diameter, from some Asian operators that would not normally send attacks. Later analysis found suspicious activity even earlier.

It has been revealed that the networks hosting SilentAir handled follow-up messages for diverted targets in odd and inconsistent ways, according to the company's technical report. That left two explanations: someone outside was faking those networks' signaling addresses, or equipment inside each network had been taken over.

In a recent development, the organization then saw equipment inside one operator both send and receive attack commands, which confirmed the second explanation. That equipment behaved exactly like SilentAir sources in other networks.

In a recent development, detecting and blocking the attacks was hard at first because the attackers understood mobile networks and signaling defenses well. After the attacks were contained, the company recovered traces of unauthorized access. It could not analyze the malware it believes SilentAir used.

Sources indicate that the report does not name the countries, the operators, or any of the targets. In some countries, SilentAir attacks came from more than one operator.

If the test text reached the hacked equipment instead of the phone, the attackers knew they were getting that person's texts.

In a recent development, most silent SMS went out at night, and most of those went to people in Taiwan. The company stated the purpose of those messages is not confirmed. They may be a bulk check that earlier diversions were still in place, since phones are least likely to re-register to their real location at night.

The silent texts carried spam-like motivational or promotional lines, often in English. The company believes the text was a disguise. If an operator along the way stripped a message's silent setting, the recipient would see it as spam and ignore it.

Industry observers note that its tracking and interception attacks also followed a working day in UTC+8, which is China Standard Time. They started at 9 a.m., almost stopped on weekends, and paused or slowed around Chinese holidays.

In a recent development, the organization also considered a link to Liminal Panda, a group behind earlier telecom intrusions. It called the link possible but unconfirmed and does not tie the two groups together for now.

Industry observers note that in several hacked operators, SilentAir attacks happened during a known Liminal Panda infection. At other times, the two revealed no sign of working together. They also went after operators in the same part of Asia, though Liminal Panda has no known focus on Taiwan.

SilentAir's behavior also partly matches that of SCTPE, a little-known Linux trojan that runs in the kernel and is designed to send and receive SS7 and Diameter traffic.

Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has described the same tool in a government advisory. There, the tool is called SIGweaver. The agency stated CrowdStrike identified it on January 21 and links it to Liminal Panda with moderate confidence.

But Enea mentioned SilentAir answered messages it had not sent itself, which the known SCTPE program cannot do. SilentAir's operational security also seemed far better than Liminal Panda's.

Separately, the organization's GTP firewall has detected Liminal Panda activity at several customer operators since the first quarter of this year. The company blocked the group's GTPDoor traffic there and saw Liminal Panda infections, or strong signs of them, in at least 5 to 10 operators.

Sources indicate that the GTPDoor backdoor, first documented on February 27, 2024, hides commands within GTP-C, the protocol that establishes mobile data connections between networks. The tech giant also found evidence of a upcoming version that hides commands in GTP-U, the part of GTP that carries customers' data. GTP-U traffic is harder to inspect, though the company believes the new version serves mainly as a backup.

The company noted any attacker could reuse these techniques, and it told operators to:.

The report does not advise people whose calls and texts may be targeted.

#92. How AIClaw 3.11.5 Separates Installed Versions from Published Release History

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (520 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How AIClaw 3.11.5 Separates Installed Versions from Published Release History

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An update screen has to answer two different questions: which version is running here, and what has actually been published?
  • Recent findings suggest that AIClaw 3.11.5 adds an About page that brings the installed version, an update check, and recent release notes into settings.
  • It has been revealed that the About view asks the existing Electron bridge for the application version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An update screen has to answer two different questions: which version is running here, and what has actually been published? A tag pushed to GitHub is not enough to answer the second question. A failed release workflow can leave a tag behind without producing a GitHub Release.

Recent findings suggest that AIClaw 3.11.5 adds an About page that brings the installed version, an update check, and recent release notes into settings. The useful part is how it keeps local version information and remote release history independent.

It has been revealed that the About view asks the existing Electron bridge for the application version. It separately loads release notes through a read-only IPC endpoint. A failed history request therefore does not prevent the page from showing the local version.

Sources indicate that the Check for updates button uses the existing upgrade action. It does not infer update availability from the list of release notes. That keeps browsing release history separate from deciding whether a newer version is available.

The release-notes reader requests the project’s public GitHub Releases endpoint with a ten-second timeout. It accepts only entries explicitly marked as neither drafts nor prereleases, with a published timestamp and a tag matching the stable vX.Y.Z form.

The implementation requests the first ten API results, filters them, and returns at most ten notes. That is a bounded recent history, not a complete archive: if the first page contains prereleases, the resulting list can have fewer than ten entries. A tag with no published release never enters this list.

Each accepted entry contains the tag, publication time, note body, and a release link. The link is constructed from the fixed AIClaw repository address and validated tag rather than copied from a response-provided URL. Note bodies are capped at 100,000 characters per entry and displayed through the existing Markdown renderer.

Sources indicate that the page has separate loading, failure, and empty states. A failed HTTP request or an invalid top-level response stays an error; it is not converted into an empty list that could misleadingly suggest there are no releases. The failure state provides a retry button. A published entry without a note body gets its own “no release notes” message.

This is still an online history view. It does not provide an offline archive, paginate through every past release, or prove that a downloaded installer has been exercised on a particular machine.

According to recent reports, the release-note tests cover stable-release filtering, fixed-repository links, and preservation of HTTP and invalid-response errors. The desktop smoke suite also checks that the About page displays the application version and release notes.

The 3.11.5 release notes report a passing local make check, including 381 work UI checks, plus release-note tests under Node 22 in a Linux container. Those checks are distinct from live acceptance of every installer. The GitHub Release itself is now publicly published.

A small About page can make version support less ambiguous: the installed version comes from the application, the history comes from published releases, and a network failure remains visible as a network failure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Cloudflare Introduces Private Origins for Application Services.

Nov 15, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare recently made Application Services for Private Origins generally available, allowing public traffic to reach applications hosted on private networks without exposing their IP addresses or opening inbound firewall ports. Private-to-private connectivity is not yet supported.

According to recent reports, unveiled in closed beta in June, the service is now generally available with a simplified configuration: private IP addresses are automatically detected in proxied DNS records, and private routing can be configured through the DNS API. Enrique Somoza, product development manager at Cloudflare, writes:.

We introduced this capability (...) to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet.

Sources indicate that existing Cloudflare connectivity can be used to apply WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, and Workers to private origins, just as with public-facing applications. The service also supports private TCP/UDP origins through Spectrum and private connectivity for Workers. Somoza adds:.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

Using Private Origins requires a Private Origins entitlement, Cloudflare One connectivity, and Unified Routing (not required when using Cloudflare Tunnel). Cloudflare WAN and Mesh connections also require return routes for Cloudflare's IPv4 (100.64.0.0/12) and IPv6 (2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64) source ranges, as well as a proxied DNS record pointing to the private IP with private network routing enabled. Existing WAF, caching, and bot management policies apply automatically. Simon Painter, cloud network consultant, notes:.

No extra connector software. WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching and Workers all sit in front of stuff that was never meant to be on the open internet. The interesting bit isn't the marketing wrapper — it's the DNS implication. For years the rule was: "if it answers a public DNS name, it's reachable from the public internet." That stops being true here.

It has been revealed that cloudflare is not the only cloud provider offering ways to connect public-facing services to private application backends. AWS, for example, offers CloudFront VPC Origins, while Microsoft provides similar capabilities through Azure Front Door Premium and Private Link. Giacomo Masseroni writes:.

Finally. been punching holes in security groups just to let the edge in.

With general availability, Cloudflare has updated the Private Origins developer documentation. The announcement does not clarify whether the feature carries an additional charge or is included in existing Enterprise contracts.

According to recent reports, cloudflare plans to extend the service to support private-to-private traffic, allowing owners, services, and AI agents on one private network to access applications on another. A closed beta is targeted for early 2027.

#88. Two quote marks took down the datacenter proxy

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (564 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

Two quote marks took down the datacenter proxy

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A proxy URL in our secret store was wrapped in typographic quotes.
  • This is how we found it, and what to do so it doesn't happen to you.
  • In a recent development, an alert fired: a queue backlog had aged past two hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A proxy URL in our secret store was wrapped in typographic quotes. Nothing could parse it, one service crash-looped on startup, and two others quietly fell back to direct HTTP. The command that wrote it looked correct, and when we copied it out of chat it worked fine.

This is how we found it, and what to do so it doesn't happen to you.

In a recent development, an alert fired: a queue backlog had aged past two hours. Every pod of the download worker was dying at startup with the same line:.

Recent findings suggest that two other services that read the same secret didn't crash. They logged a warning about an invalid proxy URL and fell back to direct HTTP, so they kept running without their datacenter proxy tier. The queue grew to about 12,000 messages while the worker restarted in a loop.

Our startup log prints a safe description of each proxy URL: host, port and zone, with no credentials. For a URL that fails to parse, it prints the word invalid.

According to recent reports, two proxy URLs are configured, a datacenter one and an unlocker one. They come from separate secret properties and are parsed by the same code. The unlocker logged a normal host and zone. Only the datacenter one logged invalid. So only one value was bad.

Recent findings suggest that our team could write the secret but not read it or its history, which is why this took a while. Once we had read access, the version history of the property highlighted it. One version was 96 characters long instead of 94, and it began and ended with these:.

A shell only treats ' and " as quoting. The curly versions are ordinary characters, so the secret store kept them.

The stored value was never a URL. It was a URL wrapped in two extra characters.

Go's net/url gives different errors depending on where the stray character sits:.

If you only check err != nil, the last row slips through, so check the host too.

The commands were kept in Apple Notes. Notes turns on Smart Quotes by default, and it converts quotes as you type, not when you paste.

Two lines in the same note can therefore differ:.

Sources indicate that the first line was pasted into the note. The second was typed by hand. The closing quote on the second line is the right curly quote, U+2019, the same character we found at the end of the stored secret.

That also explains why only one of the two commands failed. The unlocker command was pasted and stayed straight. The datacenter command had been edited by hand in the note.

In a recent development, the command was shared in a chat app, and chat apps tend to normalise quotes back to straight ones. Copying the command out of the message gave one that worked. When someone ran the original command again to show it was broken, it broke again, with the same bytes. Only the raw stored value showed the difference.

The shell, the secret store and the URL parser all did exactly what they were told. The only thing that changed was two characters that look almost the same as the ones you meant. If a value that "looks right" won't parse, look at its bytes.
