📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

According to recent reports, hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Sources indicate that rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

It has been revealed that A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about latest ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

Industry observers note that that source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. manufacturer or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot demonstrates a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

It has been revealed that the Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”.

According to recent reports, mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian firm was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it reveals the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

Industry observers note that “If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”.

It has been revealed that an email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer mentioned the organization’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”.

Industry observers note that the statement stated CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding firm led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

Recent findings suggest that experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology tech giant PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

Recent findings suggest that but that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool people, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.

It has been revealed that the FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”.

In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately noted they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo remarked. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”.

Camillo noted the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.

In a recent development, in recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

#50. How to pay for a small app build without betting on a stranger

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (826 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev

How to pay for a small app build without betting on a stranger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nearly every first call starts with the same question, and it is never phrased as a question.
  • I have been on both ends of it, as the person hiring and the person building.
  • According to recent reports, all up front.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nearly every first call starts with the same question, and it is never phrased as a question. It arrives after ten minutes of talking about the app: "So how does payment work?" What the person means is "how do I hand money to someone I met last Tuesday and still be able to walk away?".

Fair question. I have been on both ends of it, as the person hiring and the person building.

According to recent reports, all up front. A developer asks for the whole amount before starting; a client offers it to get a discount. Both are bad ideas, in opposite directions. The client's only leverage after the transfer is a polite WhatsApp message.

Fifty-fifty. The most common proposal, and it is better than nothing, but it puts the milestone in the wrong place. The first half of a build is the part everyone enjoys: screens, the flow, the thing that made the idea feel worth doing. The second half is the ugly part that takes more days than it should — and the client only finds out how ugly during delivery, with half the money already gone.

Recent findings suggest that hourly. Fine for maintenance, wrong for an app that has to reach a specific point. It rewards the work that is easy to measure, and the work that decides whether the app survives — permissions, payments, deployment, the odd failure path — is exactly the part nobody wants to be the slow billable hour.

Four steps, and only one of them involves money before anything exists.

1. The scope conversation is free and it is not a sales call. We spend it on the ugly questions: who signs in, who pays and through what, what happens when the same record is edited by two people, where the data lives, who owns the domain. At the end there is a written scope — a page, not a proposal deck — and a price. If the price is wrong for you, we stop there and it cost you nothing. On my side that is deliberate: the number should be a decision, not a negotiation tactic.

2. The deposit buys the first day or two of work, not the whole project. It is small enough that losing it would annoy you but not hurt you, and large enough that I am not working for free on a maybe. What it buys is defined in the same sentence: the first working flow, on your own accounts.

Industry observers note that 3. A walkthrough before the second payment. This is the step that replaces trust with evidence. Before any more money moves, you get a link that opens on a throwaway dataset and you click through it yourself, with your own phone, your own badly-typed email. Not a video of me clicking. Not screenshots. If what you see does not match the scope, we fix it or we stop, and stopping at that point does not require a lawyer.

Recent findings suggest that 4. The balance moves when the accounts move. The last payment is triggered by handover, not by a promise: source code in a repository you own, the database and hosting under your billing account, the domain registrar in your name, and — the one people forget — the store seller account applications, which take longer than the app did.

Two sentences in the scope prevent most of the arguments I have seen:.

On the developer's side: anyone who wants everything up front, anyone who cannot issue an invoice from a real company, anyone whose price is a range that only narrows after you have paid, and anyone who will not name the person who will actually write the code.

On the client's side: "we will pay when the app is live and making money" (that is a co-founder offer, not a contract), a scope that exists only in a chat thread, and a project that is "basically finished, just needs a few things" where nobody can list the few things. That last one is not a payment problem, it is a scoping problem, and it is the most common way a rescue job turns into an argument about whose fault the delay was.

A three-month project cannot be paid this way, because too much happens between milestones. A three-to-five day build can, and that is most of the reason the timeline is short: the shorter the build, the smaller the bet at every step, and the sooner you are clicking a real link instead of imagining one.

I build these as a one-person studio in Seoul — you talk to the person writing the code, the scope call is free, and nothing is due before there is a contract. If you have an app sitting at 80% and are trying to figure out whether a second person can finish it, that first conversation is the cheap way to find out.

Industry News: PostgreSQL Patches 52 Flaws, Including 22-Year-Old Bug Enabling Authenticated RCE

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thehackernews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server.
  • The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8.
  • In a recent development, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A type confusion flaw in PostgreSQL lets a database user who can create objects run code on the server. Updates released yesterday fix it, along with 51 other security flaws. Full protection from this flaw also requires rebuilding any C-language extensions installed on the server.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-6460, has a CVSS score of 8.8. Any code run this way has the rights of the operating system user that runs PostgreSQL. All versions before 18.7, 17.12, 16.16, 15.20, and 14.25 are affected.

In a recent development, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, which publishes the database's releases, has not reported any attacks using the flaw. CISA's assessment in the CVE record also lists exploitation as none.

The flaw involves composite types, which are types built from named fields, each with its own data type. A field's type can be changed while older values of that type are still held in other parts of the server.

Industry observers note that the server could then read an old value as if it had the new type. The fix, described in the project's release notes, adds version checks so the server can detect a value that no longer matches its type.

Security researcher Mehmet Ince described a working exploit for the flaw, demonstrated on PostgreSQL 18.6, in a technical writeup published this week.

According to recent reports, his method is to prepare a query that holds a value, change the type of one of the value's fields, and then run the query. The writeup includes the SQL that crashes an unpatched server this way and a second step that leaks memory addresses. It does not include the SQL for the final step, which makes the server run a command.

He wrote that he could "trigger this crash as a lowest-privileged login role." The project's security advisory describes the attacker only as someone who can create objects, without saying which privileges that takes.

According to recent reports, red Hat, which ships PostgreSQL packages, states in its CVE assessment that an attacker needs a database login with the ability to create or modify objects. None of these sources says whether an account with only default privileges can go beyond the crash to run code.

In a recent development, ince traces the root of the flaw to May 5, 2004, when PostgreSQL gained the ability to change a column's type. His technique for running code relies on a later change made on May 14, 2015.

Recent findings suggest that he also adapted the exploit for managed PostgreSQL services and privately shared proofs of concept with their security teams in August. The providers he worked with include AWS (Aurora and RDS), Microsoft (Azure PostgreSQL), Google (AlloyDB), Supabase, Databricks, and Ubicloud. The writeup does not give each service's current patch status.

The project credits more than a dozen reporters for CVE-2026-6460, including the researcher, and credits him on five other flaws in the same release.

The project rates 32 of the 52 flaws at 8.8, the highest score in the release. Based on the scores in its vulnerability index, only one flaw in the server requires neither a login nor any user action. That flaw, CVE-2026-116322, lets an unauthenticated client trigger a restart of PostgreSQL 18 servers.

Several other fixes are in client tools. A crafted archive can make pg_restore run code as the user running it. A compromised source server can make psql run code through the restore script in pg_dump's tar output.

CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that CSS optimization is a deceptive topic.
  • In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.
  • The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that CSS optimization is a deceptive topic. On the one hand, it feels like something simple that we should already have all the tooling for — especially when it comes to minification. On the other hand, the idea that we already exploited “everything” there is around CSS optimization may be considered naive. Such a claim looks hard to defend for a language that evolves almost daily.

In this article, I’d like to pick a technique that’s at least 18 years old — UDJO, or “using declarations just once.”.

Aware of an older source? Please comment!

The technique is inspired by the principle of DRY, “don’t repeat yourself”, in that it works by identifying and reducing (if not eliminating) declaration repetition.

So, if there’s something like display: flex and it appears two or more times, it gets reconciled in one rule:.

The outcome of the technique depends on how intelligently the deduplication is done and how long the selectors are. Intelligence determines if UDJO leads to an actual maintainability advantage — can the change of a declaration really be done to all the selectors attached? And the selector length influences how massive file size savings are.

It has been revealed that if you’re interested, my article on “DRY CSS” describes the mechanics in more detail. The question here is: Is UDJO still effective and still relevant today?

When we try to answer this question, however, we end up with a problem: When sites are complex and their style sheet declarations have not been de-duplicated before, UDJO can require a lot of work.

To save some time, I built tooling for this work. While it didn’t seem like it would immediately be as comprehensive as manually going through and testing style sheets, it seemed realistic enough that a tool could catch some repetition.

Skipping ahead, I created CSS Dedup not only to identify repetition, but also to deduplicate what could safely be optimized (CSS Dedup has some documentation on this but in essence, deduplication affects selector locations, which is part of how the cascade works). This, then, gives us some data:.

In a recent development, for the first batch, I arbitrarily picked 20 websites to analyze. I then used CSS Dedup to check what the file size changes would be if we deduplicated what seemed provably safe, and also what seemed probably safe, but only if it led to file size savings.

In a recent development, I picked those two options to provide the “natural” result of deduplication, but also the one site owners may be most interested in to reduce repetition but also decrease transfer size. After all, UDJO as a CSS optimization technique can improve both maintainability and performance.

Recent findings suggest that important note: These values cannot be used to tell CSS quality—they depend on selector length and also on verifying if deduplication, in the respective case, actually leads to better maintainability. Also note that this leaves out changes after compression—this was not part of the experiment but would be fair to test, too.

Recent findings suggest that for the question whether UDJO still works today, this should be a yes. It works as well as to even come with file size savings.

Maybe you’re curious, too, about what the situation looks like in our field, among web developers. Let’s take some samples on this, too.

It would be valuable to expand this analysis to take more samples and investigate the differences across samples, but there may be something to web professionals using shorter selectors so as to be able to benefit more from UDJO.

As mentioned at the beginning, UDJO’s effectiveness generally depends on the kind of repetition as well as on the length of selectors.

This can be managed, however: While tools like CSS Dedup make no difference between declaration use cases (and are therefore blunt), it is possible to configure them so as to reap the performance benefits.

Recent findings suggest that as the data taken for this article suggest, file size savings may be achieved in most cases. Considering that this is based on safe changes, this means a low-cost performance optimization vector — especially when applied to minified output. It’s still a good idea to couch that against the use of further compression (e.g. gzip/Brotli), but at face value, deduplication demonstrates how it can reduce the size of CSS.

It has been revealed that for anyone generally interested in CSS optimization, maintainability, and performance, UDJO should probably be part of the overall approach to CSS. But since the technique has been niche and since tooling is new, I invite you to review, test, and explore this vector. It seems hard to argue that we have reached the ceiling of how far we can take CSS optimization.

#41. OCR ไทย 4 MB ที่รันบนซีพียู: 1,000 หน้าในไม่ถึงสองนาทีจริงไหม

OCR ไทย 4 MB ที่รันบนซีพียู: 1,000 หน้าในไม่ถึงสองนาทีจริงไหม

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (311 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา).
  • โพสต์ Facebook ของ Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn อ้างว่า AI อ่านเอกสารไทยตัวจิ๋วขนาด 4 MB ทำงานแบบปิดเน็ต ไม่ใช้การ์ดจอ และอ่าน 1,000 หน้าเสร็จราวนาทีครึ่ง [1].
  • ผมไปดูโมเดลบน Hugging Face แล้ว ผลคือมีอยู่จริง และตัวเลขความเร็วก็ใกล้เคียง แต่มีเงื่อนไขที่โพสต์ไม่ได้เล่า.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | 13 พฤศจิกายน 2026.

บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา).

โพสต์ Facebook ของ Kobkrit Viriyayudhakorn อ้างว่า AI อ่านเอกสารไทยตัวจิ๋วขนาด 4 MB ทำงานแบบปิดเน็ต ไม่ใช้การ์ดจอ และอ่าน 1,000 หน้าเสร็จราวนาทีครึ่ง [1].

ตัวเลขนั้นฟังดูเกินจริงจนต้องไปเปิดต้นทาง.

ผมไปดูโมเดลบน Hugging Face แล้ว ผลคือมีอยู่จริง และตัวเลขความเร็วก็ใกล้เคียง แต่มีเงื่อนไขที่โพสต์ไม่ได้เล่า.

ชื่อเต็มคือ OpenThai2.0-OCR-Text พัฒนาโดย iApp Technology ภายใต้โครงการ OpenThai ซึ่งเดิมใช้ชื่อ OpenThaiGPT [2].

นี่คือเอนจิน OCR สำหรับข้อความพิมพ์ไทยและอังกฤษ ที่รันบนซีพียูอย่างเดียว [2].

ตัวโมเดลมีพารามิเตอร์รวม 1.02 ล้านตัว แยกเป็นตัวตรวจจับข้อความ 428,000 ตัว และตัวอ่านบรรทัด 587,000 ตัว [2].

ไฟล์มีสองก้อน คือ det.onnx ขนาด 1.8 MB และ rec.onnx ขนาด 2.4 MB รวมกันประมาณ 4.2 MB [2].

นี่คือที่มาของคำว่า 4 MB ในโพสต์.

โมเดลการ์ดระบุว่าใช้เวลา 0.39 วินาทีต่อหน้าหนาสี่เหลี่ยมหนึ่งหน้า เมื่อรันทีละหน้า [2].

และประมาณ 950 หน้าต่อนาทีบนซีพียู Xeon 8 คอร์ [2].

ถ้าคิดแบบนั้น 1,000 หน้าจะใช้เวลาราวหนึ่งนาทีกับอีกเล็กน้อย ซึ่งใกล้เคียงกับคำว่า "นาทีครึ่ง" ในโพสต์ [1].

ตัวเลข 950 หน้าต่อนาทีมาจากการรันหลายโปรเซสบนซีพียู 8 คอร์ โดยแต่ละคอร์ใช้เวลาราว 0.5 วินาทีต่อหน้า [2].

คู่มือของผู้พัฒนาให้ค่าประมาณ 0.5 วินาทีต่อหน้าบน MacBook M3 Max เช่นกัน แต่คิดต่อหนึ่งโปรเซส ซึ่งราว 120 หน้าต่อนาที [4].

แปลว่าความเร็วต่อคอร์ใกล้กัน ตัวที่ทำให้ผลต่างคือจำนวนโปรเซส.

ถ้ารันโปรเซสเดียวบน M3 Max การอ่าน 1,000 หน้าจะใช้เวลาราว 8 นาที ไม่ใช่นาทีครึ่ง.

แต่ถ้าเปิดหลายโปรเซสตามจำนวนคอร์ ตัวเลขก็เข้าใกล้ 950 หน้าต่อนาทีได้.

นี่คือเหตุผลที่คำว่า "นาทีครึ่ง" ในโพสต์ไม่ผิด แต่ขึ้นกับว่าเขารันกี่โปรเซส.

ได้ เพราะมันรันไฟล์ ONNX ในเครื่องผ่าน OpenVINO หรือ ONNX Runtime [2].

ไม่มีการเรียก API ภายนอกในขั้นตอนอ่านภาพ.

ข้อนี้สำคัญสำหรับองค์กรที่ห้ามส่งเอกสารออกนอกเครือข่าย เช่น โรงพยาบาลหรือหน่วยงานรัฐ.

แต่ต้องแยกให้ชัด การปิดเน็ตตอนรันไม่เท่ากับการปิดเน็ตตอนติดตั้ง เพราะคุณยังต้องดาวน์โหลดโมเดลและไลบรารีครั้งแรก [4].

ข้อแรก มันอ่านข้อความพิมพ์ ไม่ได้ออกแบบมาสำหรับลายมือ [2].

ข้อสอง มันคืนข้อความตามลำดับการอ่าน พร้อมกรอบและความเชื่อมั่นของแต่ละบรรทัด แต่ไม่ได้สร้างตารางหรือ Markdown [2].

ถ้าต้องการตารางหรือ Markdown ต้องใช้ OpenThai2.0-OCR-Markdown ซึ่งเป็นอีกโมเดล ขนาดไฟล์ใหญ่กว่ามาก [3].

ข้อสาม หน่วยความจำที่ใช้อยู่ราว 450 MB ต่อหนึ่งโปรเซส [2].

ถ้ารันหลายโปรเซสพร้อมกัน ตัวเลขนี้คูณตามจำนวน.

โมเดลการ์ดรายงานคะแนนเฉลี่ย 87.8 จากชุดเอกสารไทย 12 ชุด [2].

คะแนนแยกตามชุดอยู่ที่ 97.0 สำหรับคำพิพากษาศาลปกครอง, 96.3 สำหรับพระราชกิจจานุเบกษา, 99.5 สำหรับเอกสารงบประมาณ และ 77.1 สำหรับหนังสือเก่าจาก Wikisource [2].

แต่มีจุดที่ต้องอ่านให้ระวัง คือข้อมูลฝึกของโมเดลประกอบด้วยสแกนเอกสารศาล เอกสารงบประมาณรัฐสภา และหนังสือเก่าจาก Wikisource [2].

ชุดทดสอบบางชุดจึงเป็นโดเมนเดียวกับข้อมูลฝึก.

ตัวเลขสูงในกลุ่มนั้นจึงบอกได้ว่าโมเดลทำงานได้ดีกับเอกสารประเภทที่มันเคยเห็น ไม่ได้ยืนยันว่าจะเก่งเท่ากันกับใบเสร็จหรือรายงานบริษัทที่มันไม่เคยเห็น.

และการทดสอบนี้ทำโดยผู้พัฒนาโมเดลเอง ผมยังไม่เห็นงานวิจัยอิสระที่วัดกับเอกสารไทยทั่วไป.

ตัวอย่างเช่น สำนักงานบัญชีที่มีเอกสารสแกนหลายพันหน้าและต้องการค้นหาข้อความ.

การรัน OCR ในเครื่องทำให้ไม่ต้องอัปโหลดเอกสารลูกค้าขึ้นคลาวด์ ซึ่งลดความเสี่ยงด้านข้อมูลส่วนบุคคล.

แต่ต้องมีคนตรวจผลลัพธ์ เพราะ OCR ยังมีโอกาสอ่านตัวเลขหรือชื่อเฉพาะผิด.

ข้อสามสำคัญ เพราะเวลาต่อหน้าในโมเดลการ์ดวัดจากฮาร์ดแวร์ของผู้พัฒนา.

เครื่องมือแบบนี้ทำให้งานดิจิทัลไลซ์เอกสารไม่จำเป็นต้องซื้อ GPU หรือสมัครบริการคลาวด์.

แต่การประหยัดต้นทุนจะจริงก็ต่อเมื่อคุณมีคนตรวจผลลัพธ์ และมีกระบวนการเก็บไฟล์ที่ปลอดภัย.

ถ้าองค์กรคุณต้องส่งเอกสารออกไปให้บริการภายนอกอยู่แล้ว การเปลี่ยนมาใช้โมเดลในเครื่องอาจช่วยเรื่องข้อกำหนด PDPA ได้ในระดับหนึ่ง.

แต่ไม่ได้แปลว่าปลอดภัยโดยอัตโนมัติ เพราะไฟล์ต้นฉบับยังต้องถูกจัดเก็บและควบคุมการเข้าถึง.

ตัวเลข 4 MB และการรันบนซีพียูเป็นเรื่องจริง.

ส่วนคำว่า 1,000 หน้าในนาทีครึ่งเป็นผลจากฮาร์ดแวร์ที่ใช้ทดสอบ ไม่ใช่ค่าที่ทุกเครื่องจะได้.

ถ้าคุณมีงานเอกสารไทยที่ต้องอ่านซ้ำ ๆ เครื่องมือนี้คุ้มลอง เพราะต้นทุนเริ่มต้นต่ำมาก.

แต่ถ้าคุณต้องการความแม่นยำระดับใช้งานทางกฎหมายหรือการเงิน ต้องมีขั้นตอนตรวจของคนเสมอ.

คุณมีเอกสารสแกนที่ยังไม่ได้ดิจิทัลกี่แฟ้ม?

Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to upgrade their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

Industry observers note that reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare remarked it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, remarked “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security concerns in recent memory.”.

Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, stated a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”.

The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz mentioned that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the organization worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

Recent findings suggest that the PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”.

The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology manufacturer credited with finding the PHP flaws.

A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

Recent findings suggest that this is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

Sources indicate that rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

Recent findings suggest that an AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

We can call that the break-even line. Returns to customers come in three forms:.

According to recent reports, for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool reveals the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

Four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

It has been revealed that these questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

According to recent reports, run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the issue alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

Industry observers note that A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom says to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

According to recent reports, you can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Industry observers note that who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

In a recent development, compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

Sources indicate that for example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

According to recent reports, the nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

Every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

According to recent reports, error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

Automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, consumers stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

According to recent reports, map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

In a recent development, show people where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

It has been revealed that letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

Industry observers note that still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology indicates how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result showed how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Recent findings suggest that ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

In a recent development, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

According to recent reports, put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Recent findings suggest that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

Question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

It has been revealed that question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

Recent findings suggest that question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

Recent findings suggest that on Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

According to recent reports, the feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

It has been revealed that two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

Everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that new capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Sources indicate that audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that consumers might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

Recent findings suggest that the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added a high-severity security flaw impacting UnrealIRCd, an open-source Internet Relay Chat (IRC) server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-114713 (CVSS score: 8.6), is a case of improper neutralization of delimiters that could be used to execute arbitrary commands with server/IRCOp privileges.

"The labeled-response module in UnrealIRCd 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.1 does not escape the IRCv3 'label' message tag when echoing it into replies, which allows any user on a network with two or more linked servers to inject server-to-server commands that are executed with server authority," reads the description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).

The addition comes nearly a week after UnrealIRCd's project leader, developer, and maintainer, Bram Matthys (aka Syzop), released UnrealIRCd 6.2.7.1 to address multiple security vulnerabilities identified with the help of artificial intelligence, including CVE-2026-114713.

According to recent reports, "We are seeing bad guys exploiting this issue on the internet right now," Matthys noted. "Hopefully everyone has hot-patched or updated their server, or at the very least has the spamfilter workaround deployed. If not, do so ASAP!".

Recent findings suggest that exploitation attempts are mentioned to have commenced a day after the release of the hotfix on November 7, 2026. That said, the exact details of the malicious activity and its end goals are presently unknown. The maintainer described the vulnerability as the "most critical issue" found in UnrealIRCd over the past 15 years.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 16, 2026, to apply the fixes under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents across Their Lifecycle.

Nov 15, 2026 3 min read.

Sources indicate that in a recent article, Uber Engineering highlights the limitations of traditional identity and API controls in securing AI agents that dynamically reason over external content and take real-world actions. To address this challenge, Uber developed a framework to determine whether an agent's action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction.

Identity and authorization systems can determine whether a user or service has permission to access a resource, but they can't determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate in context.

This creates multiple risks, including prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions, which Uber's framework addresses through three layers spanning the entire agent lifecycle, from pre-deployment to runtime enforcement to post-deployment continuous assurance.

Industry observers note that at provisioning time, agents must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, establishing identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification. This process is automated using Argus, which analyzes the agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to identify security weaknesses. The same approach is enforced for MCP servers and tools used by the agents.

At runtime, the framework extends the traditional security model based on policy administration, policy decision, and policy enforcement to incorporate behavioral authorization, which evaluates whether an agent's actions are appropriate in a given context.

Behavioral authorization is implemented through three components: the AI Registry, AI guards, and Agent Guard runtime hooks. The AI Registry defines and manages agent policies, personas, intents, and constraints, while AI Guards evaluate interactions and proposed actions against established policies. Agent Guard runtime hooks invoke AI Guard "at critical checkpoints and applying its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed".

Industry observers note that after deployment, the focus shifts to Continuous Assurance, which relies on end-to-end observability, auditing, explainability, and replay. This layer comprises two main main components: a unified execution trace that connects agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions; and recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies and guardrails are updated to assess their effectiveness in the upcoming context.

Uber also identified several challenges in implementing security controls in production, including balancing policy restrictiveness to avoid both excessive false positives and insufficient protection, minimizing runtime latency, reducing developer friction during framework setup, and moving beyond generic controls towards agent-specific policies, which "made enforcement more contextual and precise".

Commenting on Uber's approach on LinkedIn, UN senior information technology officer Tristan G. raised several concerns, noting that while "per-agent personas, intents, constraints and calibration" is what adds the most value, they also come at a significant cost, as "the effort scales with the number of workflows". Additionally,.

By its own account, the strongest control was restricting agents to explicit constraints, which is least privilege rather than a fresh idea. For me, the open question is how this works for agents you don't build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you can't insert your own enforcement hooks.

On similar lines, AI architect Pratik Dhanave also observes that:.

The lesson they call least glamorous is the one they rate most effective: explicit intents and constraints per agent. Not generic thresholds, which failed because every agent has a different purpose and risk profile. The cost is flexibility, and they say it is worth paying.

Uber's Secure AI framework is still in evolving, with looks to expand its capabilities across all the areas outlined above. There is much more to the framework than can be covered here, so readers are encouraged to consult the ⁠original article for a more comprehensive overview.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ten objects went into a small Figma migration fixture, and ten came out in Penpot. That count was a useful first check. It did not tell us whether text stayed editable, a component instance still followed its source, or the layout behaved after resizing.

Recent findings suggest that this note describes one recorded test from November 13, 2026. It uses a deliberately small fixture and reports the differences as well as the successful checks. It is not a general compatibility verdict.

Recent findings suggest that the source contained a 600 × 420 board, two native Inter text objects, a fixed 400 × 80 horizontal auto-layout row with 12 px padding and a 16 px gap, two 120 × 40 rectangles, and a simple 100 × 48 component with a linked instance. There were ten non-root objects and one component definition.

According to recent reports, the fixture was created through the Figma plugin API. Its properties and component links were read back before export. Penpot Exporter v0.26.3 then exported all pages to a .penpot archive of 13,699 bytes. The archive was imported through Penpot's cloud interface and opened as a separate copy.

This was an exporter-to-native-archive workflow. It did not test opening a .fig file directly in Penpot.

Industry observers note that the horizontal Figma row became a Penpot Flex layout with row-reverse. The child order also reversed.

It has been revealed that reading only the direction field would make this look like an immediate ordering failure. The measured positions told a different story: rectangle A remained at (36, 132), rectangle B at (172, 132), and both stayed 120 × 40. The horizontal gap was still:.

It has been revealed that the visible order and spacing survived this conversion. The underlying layout representation changed.

A separate behavior check widened the fixed row from 400 to approximately 480 through the Penpot plugin API. The two fixed-size rectangles kept their recorded positions, dimensions and gap; the row was then restored to 400. This covers one fixed row. It says nothing about nested layouts, fill or hug sizing.

Both strings remained native text objects. Inter, weight 400 and the two recorded font sizes, 28 and 16, were retained. Their bounds changed:.

Industry observers note that to check editing, the heading was temporarily changed through the Penpot plugin API. Its width changed to 412, after which the original text was restored. That establishes an actual edit in this fixture, rather than just the presence of a text string in an exported structure.

Recent findings suggest that the dimension differences also mean this was not a pixel-identical migration. Other fonts, mixed styles and CJK text were outside the test.

The imported main object and instance pointed to the same component definition. A temporary change to the main rectangle's fill, from #1A66B2 to #2D8C51, propagated to the instance. Restoring the original fill propagated as well.

Sources indicate that this tested one same-file rectangle fill. It did not cover variants, overrides, cross-file libraries or design tokens.

After reloading the Penpot file, a further read-back confirmed the ten objects, original strings, restored 400 px row, 16 px gap, original color and component links.

According to recent reports, the Penpot MCP export_shape request for a PNG preview returned HTTP 500 / ResourceRequest timeout. The design was visible in the browser, and editor screenshots were saved, but those screenshots do not establish that server-side PNG export worked.

Recent findings suggest that the native archive import and the preview export are separate operations. The first succeeded in this fixture; the second failed. The failure's cause was not established.

It has been revealed that start with a copy containing a few features you depend on. Record source counts, text, dimensions, positions and component relationships. Export and import through the documented route, then inspect both the structure and visible geometry.

Next, make a reversible edit: change text, resize a layout container or change a component property. Check the result, restore the original state, reload, and check again. Test image export separately from import.

This fixture did not cover complex components, prototypes, collaboration, self-hosting, large production files or other versions. A successful small-file check is a starting point for deciding what to test next.

Sources indicate that the experiment was recorded for FOSS Desk, which I maintain. The Figma-to-Penpot guide includes these scoped results and their limits. The separate public software list and read-only release checker covers release metadata; it does not contain this migration fixture or its private evidence archive.

  • When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Industry observers note that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

It has been revealed that frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Recent findings suggest that still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the organization I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

In a recent development, before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the manufacturer I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

These questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional company I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Industry observers note that wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

Wheelman isn’t an ordinary tech giant, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the company, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

It has been revealed that let’s imagine I’m designing a upcoming landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Recent findings suggest that before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

Industry observers note that only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

According to recent reports, wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

Sources indicate that using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

The modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

In a recent development, the result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

In a recent development, one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

It has been revealed that wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

In a recent development, A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

Industry observers note that I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Recent findings suggest that combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

It has been revealed that the point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same firm.

It has been revealed that twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Recent findings suggest that wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

Industry observers note that and this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

That’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.
